Atopic Eczema — A Disrupted Skin Barrier

Atopic dermatitis, also called atopic eczema, is a chronic inflammatory skin disease that is not contagious. Changes in the skin barrier let moisture escape, inflammation can trigger itch, and scratching causes further damage and inflammation.

At a glance

What it is
A chronic inflammatory skin disease; not contagious
When it starts
Often in childhood, but possible at any age
Symptoms
Intense itching, dryness, cracking, scaling and thickened skin
Common sites
Elbow and knee bends and hands; babies often have it on the face
Cause
No single known cause
Outlook
Treatment can control symptoms; there is currently no cure

A barrier that lets moisture out

Skin has a protective outer layer. In atopic dermatitis, changes in this barrier allow moisture to escape and expose the skin's immune system to the environment. Genes, immune activity and environmental factors contribute, and there is no single known cause. The infographic's comparison of an intact and a disrupted surface is schematic. It illustrates moisture retention versus increased water loss, not a literal hole through the whole skin.

Inflammation can trigger itch. Scratching causes further skin damage and inflammation, and it increases the risk of bacterial infection.

Sources: [1] [3]

How it looks and feels

Symptoms include intense itching, dryness, cracking, scaling and thickened skin. Scratches may bleed or weep clear fluid. Symptoms fluctuate between flares and improvement, and itch can disturb sleep.

The appearance of eczema varies with skin tone. It can appear red, purple, gray, or lighter or darker than the surrounding skin, and inflammation may leave changes in color. Common sites include the bends of the elbows and knees and the hands, and babies often have eczema on the face. The distribution varies by age, and eczema can occur elsewhere.

Sources: [1] [2]

Family history, triggers and diagnosis

Atopic dermatitis often starts in childhood but is possible at any age. A family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever is associated with an increased likelihood, which is not proof of one cause. Soap, detergents, fragrances, rough fabrics, heat and stress may worsen symptoms, and triggers vary by person.

Diagnosis involves a clinical examination of the skin and a medical, family and trigger history. Clinicians may use tests to rule out other causes.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Daily care and treatment

Regular moisturizing, including immediately after bathing, helps the skin retain water and supports the skin barrier. Gentle cleansing with unscented or non-soap products and lukewarm water can help. The care guidance is to avoid personal irritants, keep cool and keep nails short to reduce damage from scratching, and not to change diet unless a clinician advises it.

Topical corticosteroids reduce inflammation. Clinicians may consider other topical treatments, phototherapy or systemic medicines depending on severity, age and response. These are not universal treatments. Treatment can control symptoms, but there is currently no cure. The guidance is to seek care for symptoms, or for treatments that are not helping.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Infection signs and a fire warning

Painful, warm, swollen skin, pus, sudden worsening or spreading, fever or feeling unwell, and new blisters or leaking or crusting can signal infection or eczema herpeticum. These warrant urgent medical advice.

Emollients that transfer onto clothing, bedding or dressings can make the fabrics catch fire more easily. The NHS guidance is to avoid smoking and naked flames.

Sources: [2]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Cataract — Light Through a Clouded Lens

A cataract is a clouding of the eye's natural lens, which is normally clear and bends incoming light to help vision. Most age-related cataracts develop gradually, and only surgery removes a cataract.

At a glance

What it is
Clouding of the natural lens of the eye
How it develops
Most age-related cataracts develop gradually, at variable rates
Eyes affected
One or both; cataracts do not spread between eyes
Possible symptoms
Cloudy or blurry vision, faded or yellowish colors, glare or halos, difficulty seeing at night
Removal
Only surgery, which replaces the lens with an artificial intraocular lens (IOL)

The lens and how it clouds

A cataract is a clouding of the natural lens. The lens is normally clear and bends incoming light to help vision. The cornea, iris and lens are structures at the front of the eye. The retina, the light-sensitive layer of tissue, is at the back.

Age-related changes cause proteins in the lens to break down and clump, which creates cloudy areas. Most age-related cataracts develop gradually, at variable rates. Cataracts can affect one or both eyes, but they do not spread between eyes.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Symptoms and risk factors

Cloudy or blurry vision, faded or yellowish colors, glare or halos, difficulty seeing at night, and ghosted or double images in the affected eye can occur. These symptoms can also reflect other eye problems.

Older age, smoking, diabetes, sun exposure, steroid use, family history and previous eye injury are risk factors for cataract. They do not establish a diagnosis in an individual.

Sources: [1] [2]

The eye examination

Evaluation includes visual acuity or refraction, a slit-lamp examination of the structures at the front of the eye, and a dilated examination. Dilation widens the pupil, and the eye is checked, including the retina and optic nerve at the back.

Sources: [1] [2]

Aids, surgery and protection

For mild symptoms, updated glasses, brighter reading light and magnification can help a person function, but they do not remove the cataract. Only surgery removes a cataract. The cloudy natural lens is taken out and replaced by an artificial intraocular lens (IOL).

Surgery is considered when cataracts interfere with everyday activities. Immediate surgery is not always needed, and its benefits and risks are a matter to discuss with an ophthalmologist. UV-protective sunglasses and a brimmed hat, stopping smoking, and protective eyewear can help reduce avoidable risks to the eyes. These measures do not guarantee that cataracts are prevented.

Sources: [1] [2]

Sudden changes point elsewhere

Sudden new floaters, flashes, or a curtain or shadow across vision can signal retinal detachment, not the gradual change of a cataract. The National Eye Institute guidance for these signs is to see an eye doctor or go to an emergency room immediately.

Sources: [3]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Gallstones — When Bile Flow Is Blocked

Gallstones are hard, pebble-like material formed in the gallbladder. Most are silent and cause no symptoms, but a stone that obstructs a bile duct can cause severe pain and, in some cases, complications.

At a glance

Where they form
In the gallbladder, below the liver in the upper right abdomen
Two kinds
Cholesterol stones, typically yellow-green; pigment stones, dark and made of bilirubin
Most gallstones
Silent, causing no symptoms
Pain
Can be severe and constant, upper right or middle abdomen, lasting several hours
Main treatment
Gallbladder removal for symptomatic gallstones, often laparoscopic

The gallbladder and the path of bile

The gallbladder is pear-shaped and lies below the liver in the upper right abdomen. It stores bile, which the liver produces. Bile passes through the hepatic, cystic and common bile ducts into the duodenum, and the pancreas also delivers digestive juices to the duodenum. Eating signals the gallbladder to release stored bile into the duodenum to mix with food.

Sources: [1]

How stones form

Gallstones are hard, pebble-like material formed in the gallbladder. Cholesterol stones are typically yellow-green. Pigment stones are dark and made of bilirubin. Stones may form when bile has too much cholesterol or bilirubin or not enough bile salts, or when the gallbladder empties incompletely or too infrequently. The reasons for these changes in bile are not fully understood.

Risk is higher with older age, family history, obesity and rapid weight loss, and in women. Risk factors do not establish a diagnosis in an individual.

Sources: [1] [2] [4]

Silent stones and blocked ducts

Most gallstones are silent and do not cause symptoms, and gallbladder stones without symptoms usually need no treatment. A stone that obstructs a bile duct can cause bile to build up and bring on biliary colic. Attacks often stop when the stone moves and the blockage ends.

The pain can be severe and constant, in the upper right or middle abdomen. It can last several hours and come with nausea or vomiting. Attacks often follow heavy meals. A blockage that persists can lead to gallbladder inflammation, bile-duct infection or gallstone pancreatitis. These are possible complications, not inevitable outcomes.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [4]

Evaluation, treatment and risk reduction

Evaluation of suspected gallstones can include ultrasound and blood tests. Similar symptoms may have other causes that require clinical assessment. The main treatment for gallstones that cause symptoms is removal of the gallbladder, often laparoscopic, and ERCP may clear a stone in the common bile duct. Treatment depends on clinical circumstances. After the gallbladder is removed, bile flows from the liver through the ducts directly into the duodenum instead of being stored.

Healthy eating with fiber, regular physical activity, maintaining a healthy weight and avoiding rapid weight loss can help reduce the risk of gallstones. They do not guarantee prevention, and they do not dissolve existing stones.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [4]

When urgent care is needed

The guidance is to seek urgent medical care for sudden severe abdominal pain, pain lasting several hours, fever or chills, jaundice, or pain spreading to the back with vomiting. Dark urine and pale stools may accompany complications.

Sources: [2] [4]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Iron-Deficiency Anemia — Oxygen Delivery Under Strain

Iron deficiency can impair the production of healthy red blood cells, and in the anemia that results, low hemoglobin reduces the oxygen carried from the lungs to other organs. Treatment depends on the cause and the severity.

At a glance

What happens
Low hemoglobin reduces oxygen carriage from the lungs to other organs
On a blood smear
Small red blood cells with pale centers can appear
Causes requiring evaluation
Heavy menstrual bleeding and gastrointestinal bleeding
Symptoms
There may be none when the anemia is mild or moderate
Tests
Complete blood count, ferritin and other iron studies
Common treatment
Clinician-guided oral iron, paired with treating the underlying cause

Iron, hemoglobin and oxygen

Iron deficiency can impair the production of healthy red blood cells. In anemia, low hemoglobin reduces the carriage of oxygen from the lungs to other organs. On a blood smear, iron-deficiency anemia can show small red blood cells with pale centers. A low mean cellular volume is a common laboratory finding.

Sources: [1] [2]

Blood loss, intake and absorption

Blood loss removes iron. Heavy menstrual bleeding and gastrointestinal bleeding are causes that require evaluation. A low intake of iron-containing foods can contribute, and celiac disease and stomach or intestinal surgery can impair the absorption of iron.

Sources: [1] [2]

Symptoms and testing

Mild or moderate iron-deficiency anemia may have no symptoms. More serious disease can cause fatigue, dizziness, pale skin, cold hands and feet, shortness of breath or chest pain.

Evaluation includes a medical and diet history, a complete blood count with hemoglobin and cell size, ferritin, and other iron studies. Further testing depends on the suspected cause. Low ferritin indicates reduced iron stores. Iron deficiency can occur without anemia, so hemoglobin alone does not establish the status of iron stores.

Sources: [1] [2]

Treatment and its limits

Treatment depends on cause and severity. Clinician-guided oral iron is common, and intravenous iron may be used for poor absorption, intolerance, severe deficiency or chronic blood loss. Oral iron may cause an upset stomach or constipation, and significant symptoms are a matter to discuss with the treating clinician.

Iron replacement must be paired with finding and treating the underlying cause. Transfusion is reserved for selected severe cases and does not completely correct iron deficiency. Untreated iron-deficiency anemia may lead to heart problems, pregnancy complications or developmental delays in children.

Sources: [1] [2]

Food and prevention

Beans, tofu, lean red meat, fortified cereals and dark leafy greens provide iron. Foods rich in vitamin C, such as oranges, can support absorption. Treating blood loss or absorption problems may help prevent iron-deficiency anemia. Diet supports iron intake but is not a universal substitute for treatment.

Sources: [1] [2]

Phobias · October 3, 2026

Arachnophobia — The Spider at the Curtain Fold

Arachnophobia is a fear of spiders, a type of specific phobia. The fear can be intense and out of proportion to the actual danger, and some people cannot look at a picture of a spider.

At a glance

Feared object
Spiders
Type
Specific phobia
Possible symptoms
Palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness, nausea
Why it develops
Not always clear; frightening experiences and learned fear can be involved
Treatment
CBT; exposure therapy is particularly effective for phobias

How the fear shows itself

Arachnophobia is fear of spiders, a type of specific phobia. Phobic fear can be intense and out of proportion to the actual danger. Seeing the feared object can cause immediate anxiety. Anticipating it, or even thinking about it, can also cause anxiety.

Some people with arachnophobia avoid touching a spider. Some cannot look at a picture of a spider. Physical symptoms can include palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness and nausea, and experiences vary.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Avoidance in daily life

People may actively avoid feared objects and organize their lives around avoidance, which limits daily activities. A repeated encounter can provoke anxiety again. Avoidance and intense anxiety are common features of a phobia. They are not proof of actual danger.

Sources: [1] [3]

Why a phobia develops

It is not always clear why a phobia develops. Frightening experiences can be involved, and so can learned fear.

Sources: [1] [2]

Treatment and support

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an effective treatment. Exposure therapy is a CBT method that is particularly effective for phobias. Exposure treatment can involve gradually becoming exposed to the feared object. Plans differ, and a specialist can help.

Breathing exercises and talking to a trusted person may help manage symptoms. Images of the trigger may be distressing. The sources point to a primary care provider or a qualified mental health professional when symptoms interfere with life.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Dentophobia — Waiting Beside the Dental Chair

Dentophobia is intense dental fear. Anxiety can occur before a visit, and severe, persistent fear can lead a person to avoid dental care. Ordinary nervousness does not by itself establish a phobia.

At a glance

Feared situation
Dental care
Sensory triggers
Sight of instruments, drilling sounds and vibrations, clinical smells, the reclined chair
Associated concerns
Feared pain, difficult previous experiences, unfamiliar procedures, perceived lack of control
Possible symptoms
Noticeable heartbeat, trembling, dizziness, chest tightness, feeling sick, muscle tension, sweaty palms
Approaches that can help
CBT and professionally guided exposure-based approaches

Nervousness, fear and phobia

Dental anxiety can occur before a visit. Severe, persistent dental fear can lead to avoidance. Ordinary nervousness does not by itself establish a phobia.

Dental fear can be associated with feared pain, previous difficult experiences, unfamiliar procedures or a perceived lack of control. Uncertainty about what will happen can also contribute to anxiety.

Sources: [1] [3]

Triggers and body responses

For some people, anxiety can be triggered by the sight of dental instruments, the sounds and vibrations of drilling, clinical smells and the reclined position of the dental chair.

Possible anxiety responses include a noticeable heartbeat, trembling, dizziness, chest tightness, feeling sick, muscle tension and sweaty palms. Symptoms vary.

Sources: [2] [3]

The avoidance cycle and pain

Avoiding dental care can increase the risk of dental problems and make later visits more difficult, which reinforces the fear. This is a possible cycle, not an inevitable outcome.

Fear can concern perceived danger, but concerns about pain are not to be dismissed. The sources advise patients to discuss pain management, and to tell the dentist if pain occurs even with local anesthetic.

Sources: [1] [3]

Coping at a visit

The American Dental Association's guidance for patients is to tell the dental team about anxiety and previous experiences, to ask what will happen, and to agree on a raised-hand signal to pause. Asking questions about the procedure can help reduce fear of the unknown.

The same guidance lists things that can help manage dental anxiety: headphones for bothersome drilling sounds, a handheld stress ball, slow breathing and relaxing tense muscles.

Sources: [1] [3]

Professional help

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and professionally guided exposure-based approaches can help with dental phobia. Management is tailored to the person and the clinical situation. The sources point to professional help when phobia symptoms affect life, and a dentist and a mental health professional may work together on care.

Sources: [2] [3]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Aquaphobia — At the Quiet Pool Edge

Aquaphobia is an intense fear of water or drowning. It is a separate matter from the genuine hazards of water, which are not to be dismissed as anxiety.

At a glance

Feared trigger
Water or drowning
Possible symptoms
Severe worry, noticeable heartbeat, chest tightness, trembling, nausea, dizziness
Can interfere with
Learning to swim, and daily life
Duration
Can persist into adulthood
Established treatment
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)
Genuine water hazards
Currents, waves, hidden rocks or vegetation, limited visibility

Fear of water

Aquaphobia is an intense fear of water or drowning. A specific phobia involves fear that is out of proportion to the actual danger in a particular situation. Fear of water can come with exposure to water, with thoughts of water, and with reluctance to enter water or to immerse the face or body. Individual experiences vary. Fear of water can interfere with learning to swim, and it can persist into adulthood.

Unfamiliar things a person perceives in the water can accompany anxiety. A small exploratory study described concerns about depth, about locating the surface and about finding solid support. These are illustrative concerns. They are not universal symptoms, and they are not a safety assessment.

Sources: [1] [4]

Symptoms and avoidance

Phobia symptoms can include severe worry, a noticeable heartbeat, chest tightness, trembling, nausea and dizziness. Not everyone has every symptom.

Anticipating or encountering a feared situation can bring intense anxiety and active avoidance, and phobias may interfere with daily life. The infographic shows a sequence of repeated encounters and avoidance. The sequence is an illustration, not a universal account of cause or a diagnosis.

Sources: [1] [2]

Genuine hazards and precautions

Natural water may have currents, waves, hidden rocks or vegetation, and limited visibility. Genuine hazards are not to be dismissed as anxiety.

Drowning prevention guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says swimming lessons can reduce drowning risk, and that swimming with a buddy and choosing lifeguarded sites when possible remain important precautions. Life jackets reduce drowning risk while boating and can help weaker swimmers around natural water and pools. Inflatable or foam toys are not safety devices.

Sources: [3]

Treatment and support

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an established treatment for phobias, and exposure therapy is a particularly effective CBT method. Healthcare professionals can help determine next steps. The infographic gives no treatment protocol for entering water. Its scenes are illustrative, not a diagnosis or an instruction to enter water.

The sources point to a healthcare professional if symptoms affect life. Breathing exercises and talking to someone trusted can help manage symptoms. Managing anxiety does not replace water safety.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Pyrophobia — The Candle Behind Glass

Pyrophobia is an intense fear of fire. Within the framework of specific phobias, the fear is out of proportion to the actual danger, while ordinary fire precautions remain necessary.

At a glance

Feared trigger
Fire
Framework
Specific phobia
Possible symptoms
Palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness, nausea
Treatment

Candle clearance

Fire as a phobia trigger

Specific phobias involve intense fear that is out of proportion to the actual danger. The infographic applies that framework to fear of fire. Anticipating a feared object or situation can cause excessive worry, and encountering it can cause immediate, intense anxiety.

Phobia symptoms can include palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness and nausea. People may actively avoid feared objects and situations, or endure them with intense anxiety. Avoidance can restrict activities.

Sources: [1] [2]

Actual fire risk from candles

Open flames are dangerous if candles tip over or are too close to combustible objects, and ordinary fire precautions remain necessary.

The U.S. Fire Administration's candle guidance suggests considering battery-operated flameless candles. Lit candles need stable holders, need to be at least 12 inches from anything that burns, and are extinguished when a person leaves the room or before bed. For a power outage, the guidance is to use flashlights, not candles.

Sources: [3]

Therapy and support

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) teaches different ways of thinking, behaving and reacting. Exposure therapy is particularly effective for phobias. Exposure-based CBT helps people engage in activities and situations they have avoided, and relaxation exercises may accompany it.

Breathing exercises and talking to a trusted person may help manage symptoms. The sources point to a primary care provider when symptoms affect life. A provider can refer a person to a qualified mental health professional.

Sources: [1] [2]

Earth & space · October 6, 2026

Aurora — From Magnetosphere to Photon

An aurora is light released by oxygen and nitrogen in the upper atmosphere after electrons accelerated in Earth's magnetosphere collide with them. The energy enters the magnetosphere from the solar wind.

At a glance

Energy source
The solar wind, which transfers energy into Earth's magnetosphere
What strikes the air
Electrons accelerated within the magnetosphere
Oxygen light
Green and red
Nitrogen light
Blue and pink-purple
Shape
Ovals around the magnetic poles

Energy from the solar wind

The solar wind transfers energy into Earth's magnetosphere, and the pressure of the solar wind stretches a magnetotail away from the Sun. Energy transfer through magnetic reconnection is favored when the magnetic field of the solar wind and the magnetic field of Earth point in opposite directions.

Auroral electrons are accelerated within the magnetosphere. The electrons of a nighttime aurora can come from the magnetotail, rather than arriving directly as solar-wind electrons. The accelerated electrons follow magnetic field lines into the upper atmosphere near the magnetic poles.

Sources: [1] [2]

How the light and colors arise

Collisions transfer energy from the electrons to atoms and molecules in the atmosphere, exciting them. When they relax, they release photons. Excited atomic oxygen produces green and red light. Nitrogen can produce blue and pink-purple light.

Red oxygen light is favored higher up, where the atmosphere is thinner. Green oxygen light and the pink-purple nitrogen lower borders can occur below it. These are tendencies, not rigid altitude boundaries. The excited state of oxygen that produces red light lasts longer than the state that produces green. In the denser air lower down, collisions can quench the red emission before a photon is emitted.

Sources: [1] [2]

Ovals, arcs and curls

Auroral emissions form ovals around the magnetic poles, not a single spot over the geographic pole. Quiet displays can be simple arcs. Greater geomagnetic activity can yield brighter multiple arcs, rays, waves and curls, and can expand the oval toward lower latitudes.

Sources: [2]

What eyes and cameras see

Cameras can detect auroral colors that are too dim for human eyes. A faint aurora may look pale to a person because night vision favors brightness over color.

Sources: [1] [2]

Burying Beetle — A Nursery Beneath the Soil

Nicrophorus vespilloides is a burying beetle that turns the carcass of a small vertebrate into an underground nursery. Parents strip, roll and bury it, smear it with fluids that inhibit microbial growth, and can feed their larvae.

At a glance

Scientific name
Nicrophorus vespilloides
Family
Silphidae
Breeding resource
Small vertebrate carrion
Markings
Orange markings across dark, shortened wing covers
Parental care
By both parents or by a single parent
Studied populations
Woodland west of Cambridge, England

Recognizing the adult

Nicrophorus vespilloides is a burying beetle in the genus Nicrophorus and the family Silphidae. The adult specimen in the reference photograph has a black head and pronotum, black clubbed antennae and six jointed legs. Its wing covers are dark and shortened, with orange markings running across them, and the tip of the abdomen is exposed.

The species occurs in woodland populations west of Cambridge, England. The leaf litter and soil in the infographic stand for that kind of woodland. They are not a map of the full range.

Sources: [1] [3] [4]

Finding and burying a carcass

Adults locate the carrion of small vertebrates, and flight is part of how they find it. The carcass serves as both the breeding resource and the food for their offspring. Parents remove the fur or feathers, roll the flesh into a ball and bury the prepared carcass in an underground chamber.

Carrion is a scarce resource, and beetles compete over it. They use their mandibles in contests. Larger individuals often have the advantage, but they are not guaranteed to win.

Sources: [1] [4] [5]

Keeping microbes in check

Parents smear the carcass with exudates that inhibit microbial growth. This is known as social immunity. It does not sterilize the carcass completely.

Lysozymes, which are antimicrobial enzymes, are implicated in social immunity. In females, the antimicrobial properties of the anal exudate correlate with the expression of one particular lysozyme gene. The infographic does not illustrate a specific molecular reaction.

Sources: [2]

Feeding and raising the larvae

After hatching, the larvae feed on the prepared carcass and can also receive regurgitated meat from their parents. The mouth-to-mouth contact in the infographic is feeding, not an attack. Care by both parents and care by a single parent both occur in this species, so the pair shown is one possible family arrangement, not an obligation.

Larvae disperse from the carrion to pupate and later emerge as adults. The life-history strip is schematic and not to scale, and it gives no fixed timing or brood size. In this way the beetles turn vertebrate carrion into food for growing offspring. The infographic makes no broader, quantified statement about recycling.

Sources: [1] [5]

Chrysis ignita — The Armored Curl

Chrysis ignita is a cuckoo wasp 5 to 10 mm long, with a shiny blue, green and golden red body. Cuckoo wasps have tough, heavily sculptured exoskeletons, and most of the Chrysidinae can curl into a defensive ball.

At a glance

Scientific name
Chrysis ignita
Kind of insect
Cuckoo wasp
Body length
5 to 10 mm
Range
Western Europe to central Asia and China
Habitat
Gardens, parks and forest margins
Host
Uncertain; Ancistrocerus parietum is only a probable host

Colors and surface sculpture

Chrysis ignita has a body length of 5 to 10 mm, so every close-up view in the infographic is enlarged. The head and the mesosoma, the middle section of the body, are shiny blue or violet, with green reflections on the pronotum and mesoscutellum. The tergites, the upper plates of the abdomen, are golden red. The sternites, the lower plates, are green or blue.

The pits on the mesoscutum are the same color as the surface between them. Tergites T2 and T3 have coarse, regular pitting and sharply produced teeth at the tip. The ridge across the front of the head, the frontal carina, is shallowly M-shaped or arched. It does not take the form of four tooth-like bumps.

Chrysis ignita has close lookalikes, which complicate identification. The infographic shows the frontal ridge, the sculptured body and the wings as anatomical views, not as proof that the species can be identified from color alone.

Sources: [1] [2]

Where it is found

The species occurs from western Europe to central Asia and China. Distribution records can be confused by identifications that have not been revised. Its habitats include gardens, parks and forest margins. Adults occur on old wooden or stone walls, dead tree trunks, poles and log piles.

Sources: [1]

Armor and the defensive curl

Cuckoo wasps have an abdomen that is hollowed on the underside. Most Chrysidinae can curl into a defensive ball, a behavior called conglobulation. Females that are disturbed or attacked fold into a compact ball, which shields vulnerable body parts. The curl is described at the level of the family, not for this species alone.

The exoskeletons of cuckoo wasps are heavily sculptured and very tough, and they serve as armor against the stings of hosts. This is protection, not invulnerability.

Sources: [2] [3]

Uncertain hosts and family-level development

At the level of the family, the stages of a cuckoo wasp include egg, larva, cocoon or pupa, and adult. Many cuckoo wasps develop in the nests of solitary wasps or bees, as parasitoids or as consumers of the food the host stored. Exact feeding habits differ among species.

For Chrysis ignita itself, the hosts are uncertain. Ancistrocerus parietum is only a probable host. Numerous earlier host records are unreliable because the taxonomy was inconsistent, and the close lookalikes complicate older host records.

Coccolithophores — Building Ocean Chalk

Coccolithophores are single-celled marine algae that form microscopic calcite plates inside the cell and push them out to make an overlapping outer covering. Carbonate from their plates contributes to seafloor sediment.

At a glance

What they are
Unicellular marine planktonic algae
Where they live
The upper ocean
Plates
Coccoliths, microscopic plates of calcite (CaCO3)
Where plates form
Inside the cell, in the coccolith vesicle
Outer covering
The coccosphere, made of overlapping coccoliths
In a bloom
Dense clouds of coccoliths can make water look opaque turquoise

Algae with a covering of plates

Coccolithophores are single-celled algae that live as plankton in the upper ocean. Their photosynthesis produces organic carbon, and their calcification produces inorganic carbon. The plates they make, called coccoliths, are microscopic plates of calcium carbonate in the form of calcite, CaCO3.

Sources: [1] [2]

How a plate is built

Coccoliths are formed inside the cell, generally one at a time, in a compartment called the coccolith vesicle. Formation begins with a ring, the protococcolith ring, at the edge of an organic base-plate scale. Completed coccoliths are pushed out of the cell and form an overlapping external covering called a coccosphere.

Coccoliths of the Noelaerhabdaceae have multiple calcite crystal segments distributed radially around a central grid, and they have proximal and distal shields. Coccolith size and mass vary among species and even within a single coccosphere. The study behind these details used three-dimensional X-ray imaging to separate the plates and measure their geometry.

Sources: [2]

Plates in the water and on the seafloor

Additional coccoliths enter the surrounding seawater when cells multiply, die or produce excess plates. Dense clouds of coccoliths can give the water of a bloom an opaque turquoise appearance.

Coccolith carbonate contributes to seafloor sediment. This does not mean that every plate reaches the bottom, and it does not imply a net benefit for the climate.

The cells and plates are microscopic. The infographic shows them strongly enlarged and not to a common scale.

Sources: [1] [2]

Giant Salmonfly — Gills Beneath the Current

The giant salmonfly is a stonefly of western North American rivers. Its large nymph spends multiple years on the river bottom, with gill tufts under its thorax, shredding leaves before it climbs out of the water and molts into a winged adult.

At a glance

Scientific name
Pteronarcys californica
Group
Stoneflies (order Plecoptera), family Pteronarcyidae
Range
Western North American rivers, including the Coast, Cascade, Rocky and Sierra Nevada ranges
Nymph habitat
River bottom among cobbles, in swift, well-oxygenated water
Nymph food
Leaves and other large organic material
Adult colors
Orange or red band behind the head and under the abdomen

Gills under the thorax

The nymph's tracheal gill tufts sit on the underside of its thoracic segments. The filaments of these tufts are part of the respiratory system that takes up and delivers oxygen. Nymphs live on the river bottom among cobbles, in swift, well-oxygenated water.

Warming and low oxygen can interact to affect the nymph's physiology. The responses vary with the population and the conditions, and no universal threshold is given.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

A shredder on the river bottom

Nymphs are shredders. They feed on leaves and other large organic material collected among rocks or debris, and this feeding processes organic material. Salmonflies are in turn food for aquatic and terrestrial consumers, including trout and insect-eating birds.

The species occurs in western North American rivers, including those of the Coast, Cascade, Rocky and Sierra Nevada mountain ranges.

Sources: [1] [3]

From the water to the air

The aquatic nymph is a large-bodied insect, and the adult is winged and lives on land. The infographic shows both enlarged, not life-size. Nymphs spend multiple years in the water and grow through repeated molts. The length of this stage varies, so no single duration is given.

Mature nymphs crawl to shore and climb out of the water before the final molt into adults. Adults have an orange or red band behind the head, an orange or red underside to the abdomen, and broad wings with dark veins. Females lay their eggs on or above the water. The eggs separate and sink to the bottom, where the next generation begins.

Sources: [1] [3]

Tsunami — The Shoaling Water Column

A tsunami moves through the whole depth of the ocean. In deep water it has a long wavelength and often a small height. As it enters shallow coastal water it slows, its wavelength shortens and it can grow much taller.

At a glance

Depth of motion
The entire water depth
In the deep ocean
Long wavelength and often small surface height
Speed
Depends on water depth: faster in deeper water, slower in shallower water
Near the coast
Shorter wavelength, larger amplitude and stronger currents
Shoaling
The increase in wave amplitude as a wave moves into shallow water
Run-up
Maximum height reached inland above normal sea level

A wave through the whole water column

A tsunami propagates through the entire depth of the water. Wind waves are different: their motion is concentrated near the surface. In the deep ocean a tsunami has a long wavelength and often a small surface height, and it may be barely noticeable.

Sources: [1] [2]

Speed, depth and wavelength

The speed at which a tsunami propagates depends on the depth of the water. Deeper water permits faster propagation, and shallower water slows it. For a long wave, the propagation speed c is approximated by the square root of g times h, where g is gravitational acceleration and h is the water depth.

As a tsunami enters shallower water, its wavelength decreases. Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength. Slowing down does not in itself change the frequency, so the wavelength becomes shorter.

Sources: [1] [2]

Shoaling near the coast

Shoaling is the increase in wave amplitude as a wave moves into shallow water. Tsunami waves can grow much taller near the coast, and currents intensify as a tsunami approaches shallow coastal water.

Even after shoaling, the wavelength of a tsunami remains relatively long, and water can continue flowing inland for many minutes. Run-up is the maximum height reached inland above normal sea level. It is distinct from inundation, the horizontal extent of the flooding.

Sources: [1] [2]

Deep Vein Thrombosis — Flow Meets a Clot

Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the lower leg, thigh or pelvis. A clot may restrict the return of blood to the heart, and a clot that detaches can travel to the lungs.

At a glance

What it is
A blood clot in a deep vein
Usual location
Lower leg, thigh or pelvis; it can also occur in the arm
Possible symptoms
Swelling, pain or tenderness, warmth, redness or discoloration
Without symptoms
DVT can occur without symptoms
Pulmonary embolism
A detached clot travels through the heart and blocks blood flow in the lungs
Anticoagulants
Prevent a clot from growing or spreading and prevent new clots

A clot in a deep vein

DVT is a blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the lower leg, thigh or pelvis. It can also occur in the arm. Veins return blood from the limbs and organs to the heart, and a clot in a vein may restrict that return and cause pain and swelling.

Platelets and plasma proteins cooperate in forming clots. Dangerous clots may form inside vessels without an obvious injury, or may fail to dissolve naturally.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

What raises the risk

Slow blood flow from limited movement, and injury to veins, can increase the risk of DVT. Surgery and major injury are associated with a higher risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE), and increased estrogen and family history can raise it as well. Risk factors do not establish a diagnosis.

Sources: [1] [3]

Symptoms and diagnosis

Symptoms of DVT can include swelling, pain or tenderness, warmth, and redness or discoloration in the affected leg or arm. DVT can also occur without symptoms. Possible symptoms require prompt medical evaluation, and special medical tests are needed to diagnose DVT or pulmonary embolism (PE).

Sources: [1]

When a clot reaches the lungs

A clot that detaches from a vein can travel through the heart to the lungs and block pulmonary blood flow. This is a pulmonary embolism. Difficulty breathing, chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing, coughing blood, or fainting can be signs of PE and require immediate medical help. PE can occur without symptoms of DVT.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Treatment, risk reduction and later effects

Anticoagulants prevent a clot from growing or spreading and prevent new clots. Clot-dissolving medicines or clot removal are used in selected situations, not for everyone. Movement after confinement and leg exercises during long sitting can help reduce risk. Preventive medicines or compression stockings are individualized and are a matter to discuss with a clinician.

Damage to vein valves after DVT can cause post-thrombotic syndrome, with persistent swelling, pain, skin discoloration or, in severe cases, ulcers.

Sources: [1] [2]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Glaucoma — Protecting the Optic Nerve

Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve at the back of the eye. Reducing eye pressure aims to limit further nerve damage, and vision that has been lost cannot be restored by glaucoma treatment.

At a glance

What it is
A group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve
Open-angle glaucoma
Develops gradually; painless, often with no obvious early symptoms
Angle-closure glaucoma
The iris can block the drainage angle; sudden complete blockage is an emergency
Later effects
Peripheral vision loss and blind spots
Risk factors
Older age, a family history of glaucoma and high eye pressure
Lost vision
Cannot be restored by glaucoma treatment

Fluid, pressure and the optic nerve

Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve at the back of the eye. The optic nerve contains many nerve fibers, and loss of these fibers causes blind spots. Aqueous fluid in the front of the eye normally leaves through the drainage angle. Impaired drainage can increase eye pressure.

High eye pressure increases risk, but some people with high pressure do not develop glaucoma, and some have glaucoma at normal pressure. Older age, a family history of glaucoma and high eye pressure are risk factors, not guarantees of disease.

Sources: [1] [2]

Open-angle and angle-closure glaucoma

Open-angle glaucoma develops gradually when the eye does not drain fluid well even though the angle is open. It is painless and often has no obvious early symptoms. Later glaucoma can cause loss of peripheral vision and blind spots. The field loss pictured in the infographic is illustrative and variable, not a diagnostic simulation.

In angle-closure glaucoma, the iris can block the drainage angle. A sudden complete blockage can raise eye pressure rapidly and is an emergency. Sudden intense eye pain, a red eye, blurred vision or nausea can signal angle closure, and halos, headache and vomiting can occur. The guidance for these signs is to seek urgent eye care or emergency care immediately.

Sources: [1] [2]

How glaucoma is found

Diagnosis needs a comprehensive eye examination. Pressure alone is insufficient. The examination includes assessment of the optic nerve, visual field testing and inspection of the drainage angle, and corneal thickness may be measured.

Sources: [1] [2]

Lowering eye pressure

Prescription drops lower pressure by reducing the production of aqueous fluid or improving its outflow. The choice of treatment depends on the person and the type of disease. Laser trabeculoplasty improves drainage in open-angle glaucoma, and laser iridotomy makes a small opening in the iris for angle-closure glaucoma. Glaucoma surgery can create a new drainage route or use a drainage tube. Reducing pressure aims to limit further nerve damage, not to restore lost vision.

The care guidance is to follow the prescribed treatment, report side effects, attend regular follow-up, and not stop glaucoma medicines without discussing it with the ophthalmologist.

Sources: [1] [2]

Retinal Detachment — The Lifting Light Layer

Retinal detachment separates the light-sensitive retina from its normal position at the back wall of the eye and from the blood supply beneath it. It is a medical emergency that risks permanent vision loss.

At a glance

What detaches
The retina, the light-sensitive tissue lining the back of the eye
Most common type
Tear-related (rhegmatogenous)
Warning signs
Sudden increase in floaters, flashes of light, a dark curtain or shadow
Urgency
A medical emergency
Diagnosis
Dilated eye exam; OCT or ultrasound when more information is needed
Repair methods
Laser or freezing, scleral buckle, vitrectomy, pneumatic retinopexy

What the retina does

The retina is light-sensitive tissue that lines the back of the eye. It converts the light entering the eye into electrical signals, which are sent to the brain through the optic nerve. A detachment separates the retina from its normal position at the back wall and from the underlying blood supply. That impairs its function and risks permanent vision loss.

Sources: [1] [2]

How a retina detaches

The most common type is tear-related, or rhegmatogenous. Fluid passes through a hole or tear in the retina and collects beneath it, lifting it away. Aging-related separation of the vitreous gel from the retina can cause a retinal tear. Thinning of the peripheral retina and trauma can also lead to tears.

A tractional detachment occurs when scar tissue pulls the retina away. Diabetes or other conditions can cause it. An exudative detachment occurs when leaking vessels allow fluid to accumulate beneath the retina. Inflammation or abnormal vessels can be involved.

Sources: [2]

Warning signs and risk factors

Warning signs include a sudden increase in floaters, flashes of light, and a dark curtain or shadow in the field of vision. Some small detachments cause no symptoms. Retinal detachment is a medical emergency. Symptoms require an eye doctor or an emergency room right away, and prompt treatment can help protect vision.

Risk factors include extreme nearsightedness, advancing age, previous eye surgery, serious eye injury, a previous detachment and family history. Risk factors do not mean that a detachment is inevitable.

Sources: [1] [2]

Diagnosis and repair

Diagnosis uses a dilated eye exam to inspect the retina, including its periphery. OCT or ultrasound may help when more information is needed. Laser or freezing treatment can seal retinal tears, and a larger detachment may require surgery to put the retina back into place.

A scleral buckle is a silicone band outside the wall of the eye that pushes the wall closer to a retinal tear, while freezing treatment seals the tear. Vitrectomy removes the vitreous gel and drains fluid from beneath the retina. Laser or freezing seals the tears, and a gas bubble can hold the retina while it heals. Pneumatic retinopexy uses a gas bubble and a specific head posture to position the bubble over a tear, with laser or freezing to seal it.

A retina specialist selects the treatment based on the detachment. More than one procedure may be needed, and reattachment does not guarantee complete visual recovery. The macula is the center of the retina, and involvement of this central area affects the outlook for vision.

Sources: [1] [2]

Limits of prevention

Many aging-related detachments cannot be prevented. Protective eyewear during risky activities reduces the risk of injury, and regular dilated eye exams can find small tears or detachments early.

Sources: [1]

Shingles — A Nerve Awakens

Shingles, or herpes zoster, is caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus, the same virus that causes chickenpox. The reactivated virus travels in a specific nerve and commonly produces a band of rash on one side of the trunk.

At a glance

Also called
Herpes zoster
Cause
Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus, which also causes chickenpox
Typical rash
A band on one side of the trunk; the face can also be affected
Risk increases with
Older age and weakened immunity
Postherpetic neuralgia
Pain that persists in the affected area after the rash has gone
Vaccine
CDC recommends two doses of recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) for certain adults

A virus that stays in nerve cells

Shingles is caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV), the same virus that causes chickenpox. After recovery from chickenpox, the virus remains inactive in some nerve cells and may reactivate later. Why reactivation occurs in some people is not fully understood. The reactivated virus travels in a specific nerve, commonly producing a band of rash on one side of the trunk. The face can also be affected. Risk increases with older age and with weakened immunity, including from certain diseases and immune-suppressing medicines.

Sources: [1] [2]

How the rash develops

Burning or tingling pain, itching or numbness may come before a red rash. Fluid-filled blisters then dry and crust, and the scabs later clear. The timing varies. Shingles may be painful or itchy, and in some people a light touch can provoke intense pain.

Postherpetic neuralgia is pain that persists in the affected area after the rash has gone. Older people have a greater chance of developing it. Blisters on the face require prompt medical attention. Blisters near or in the eye can cause lasting eye damage and blindness.

Sources: [1] [2]

Treatment and comfort

The guidance when shingles is suspected is to contact a clinician as soon as possible. Early antiviral treatment can shorten the illness and reduce its severity, and pain relief may help. Cool washcloths, loose clothing, keeping the area clean and avoiding scratching can help with comfort and skin care.

Sources: [1] [2]

How the virus spreads

A person cannot catch shingles from another person with shingles. VZV can spread from shingles blisters to susceptible people and cause chickenpox. Spread can occur by direct contact with blister fluid or by breathing virus particles from the blisters. The virus is not spread before blisters appear or after the rash scabs over.

The CDC guidance is to cover the rash, avoid touching or scratching it, and wash hands. It also says to avoid contact with susceptible pregnant people, premature or low-birth-weight infants and immunocompromised people until the rash scabs over.

Sources: [1] [2]

Vaccination

CDC recommends two doses of recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) for adults age 50 and older, and for adults age 19 and older with immune systems weakened by disease or therapy. The aim is to prevent shingles and related complications.

Sources: [1]

Ailurophobia — A Cat Across the Landing

Ailurophobia is a fear of cats, an animal-focused specific phobia. The fear can be intense and out of proportion to actual danger, and its symptoms can interfere with daily life.

At a glance

Meaning
Fear of cats
Type
Animal-focused specific phobia
Possible triggers
Encountering or thinking about a cat; examples, not universal triggers
Possible body signs
Pounding heart, shaking, sweating, tight muscles, dizziness, nausea; not the same for everyone
Approaches that can help
CBT and gradual exposure under controlled circumstances, at an individual pace

What ailurophobia means

Ailurophobia means fear of cats. It is an animal-focused specific phobia. Phobic fear can be intense and out of proportion to actual danger, and the symptoms can interfere with daily life.

Feeling afraid is not itself a measure of actual danger. The infographic illustrates the fear with a fictional encounter with a cat on a stair landing. That scene is made up, and it does not prove that any animal is safe.

Sources: [1] [2] [4]

Triggers, thoughts and body alarm

Encountering a feared animal, or thinking about one, can trigger anxiety. Meeting a cat and anticipating a meeting are the examples illustrated. They are not triggers that every person has.

Phobic thinking can overestimate harm, or how likely it is that the feared object will be encountered, and can underestimate a person's ability to cope. The next event may be imagined as threatening.

Body alarm may include a pounding heart, shaking, sweating, tight muscles, dizziness and nausea. Not everyone experiences the same symptoms.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [4]

How avoidance keeps the fear going

Avoidance can quickly reduce anxiety. It can also prevent a person from learning that a situation can be manageable, and that maintains the phobic fear. Avoidance can change the routes a person takes and interfere with social activities and everyday life.

Sources: [2] [4]

Support and treatment

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and gradual exposure, under controlled circumstances and at an individual pace, can help specific phobias. Breathing exercises and talking to a trusted person can help manage anxiety. Professional support is relevant when fear affects daily life.

The treatment scene on the infographic is conceptual. It is not an instruction to approach, touch, restrain or provoke an animal, and care planning is individualized.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Insect Phobia — The Moth Beyond the Glass

Insects can be the focus of a specific animal phobia. The fear is intense and out of proportion to the actual danger, which makes it more than ordinary dislike.

At a glance

Feared object
Insects
Type
Specific animal phobia
Possible symptoms
Palpitations, chest tightness, nausea, trembling, dizziness, severe worry
Effect of avoidance
Can limit daily activities
Treatment
CBT; exposure therapy is particularly effective for phobias

More than ordinary dislike

Insects can be the focus of a specific animal phobia. Phobic fear is intense and out of proportion to the actual danger. It is more than ordinary dislike.

Anticipating or thinking about the feared object can provoke intense anxiety, and encountering it can also trigger anxiety. The infographic uses a moth of ordinary size on the far side of glass as a fictional example. The scene is illustrative, not diagnostic.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Symptoms and avoidance

Symptoms can include palpitations, chest tightness, nausea, trembling, dizziness and severe worry. Symptoms vary. People with phobias may actively avoid feared objects and situations, or endure them with intense anxiety. Avoiding the feared object can limit daily activities and lead people to organize their lives around avoiding their fear.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Treatment and support

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) teaches different ways of thinking, behaving and reacting to reduce fear and anxiety. Exposure therapy is a CBT method that is particularly effective for phobias. Treatment for a simple phobia can involve gradually becoming exposed to the feared object. Treatment is individualized, and a qualified mental health professional can help plan next steps.

Breathing exercises, talking with a trusted person and support groups can help manage symptoms. The NHS sources point to professional help when phobia symptoms interfere with everyday life.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Ornithophobia is a phobia of birds, an animal-type specific phobia. The fear is intense and out of proportion to the actual danger, and the avoidance and distress can interfere with life.

Birds

Animal-type specific phobia

Fear of birds

Ornithophobia means phobia of birds. It is an animal-type specific phobia. Specific phobias involve intense fear that is out of proportion to the actual danger, and the avoidance and distress can interfere with life.

Encountering, anticipating or thinking about a feared object can produce anxiety. Pictures can also trigger fear in some people. The bird pictures and the courtyard encounter in the infographic are illustrative examples, not universal triggers.

A frightening event or learned responses may contribute to phobias, but a clear cause is not always identifiable.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Predictions and the body's alarm

People may overestimate the danger and underestimate their ability to cope. Uncertainty about a feared encounter may fuel anxious predictions.

Possible physical symptoms include a fast heartbeat, sweating, trembling, tense muscles, dizziness, chest tightness and nausea. Symptoms vary between people. Physical alarm prepares the body for possible danger, the fight-or-flight response. Alarm does not by itself prove that the feared situation is dangerous.

Sources: [1] [3]

How avoidance maintains the fear

Avoidance can reduce anxiety quickly. It also prevents opportunities to revise feared predictions, and it can maintain the phobia. Repeated avoidance can restrict everyday activities. In the infographic, skipping the courtyard is a fictional example of that effect.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Therapy and support

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) examines unhelpful thoughts and habits. Graded exposure uses small, manageable steps, and therapist-assisted exposure can treat specific phobias. The steps are chosen for the individual. They are not a universal exposure prescription.

Talking to someone trusted and practicing relaxing breathing may help. The sources point to professional help if fear affects daily life. The scenes in the infographic are fictional educational illustrations, not a diagnosis and not instructions to approach or handle birds.

Appendicitis — The Inflamed Cul-de-sac

Appendicitis is an infected, swollen appendix, a small pouch attached to the bowel in the lower right abdomen. Symptoms and the location of pain vary, and suspected appendicitis requires immediate medical assessment.

At a glance

The appendix
A small pouch attached to the bowel in the lower right abdomen
Appendicitis
An infected, swollen appendix
Pain
May start around the belly button and move to the lower right
Cause
Unclear in many cases
Usual treatment
Surgical removal of the appendix (appendectomy), with antibiotics

The appendix and possible causes

The appendix is a small pouch attached to the bowel in the lower right abdomen. Appendicitis means an infected, swollen appendix. Possible causes are blockage by hardened stool or enlarged tissue in the wall of the appendix. In many cases the cause is unclear.

Sources: [1] [2]

How the pain changes

Abdominal pain may start around the belly button and move to the lower right. It may worsen over hours and worsen with movement or coughing. Loss of appetite, nausea or vomiting, and fever may occur. Not everyone has the typical symptoms or the typical location of pain.

Sources: [1] [2]

Urgent assessment and diagnosis

Suspected appendicitis requires immediate medical assessment. Severe abdominal pain, confusion or difficulty breathing require emergency care. Untreated appendicitis can lead to a burst appendix, peritonitis, an abscess or sepsis. These are possible complications, not inevitable outcomes.

Diagnosis uses clinical assessment and may include blood and urine tests, ultrasound or CT. No single test always identifies appendicitis, and other conditions can cause similar pain.

Sources: [1] [2]

Surgery and antibiotics

The usual treatment is surgical removal of the appendix, called an appendectomy, with antibiotics. Selected mild cases may be treated with antibiotics alone under medical supervision, but surgery remains standard care.

Sources: [2] [3]

Cat Atlas — Body Language

Cats signal with their ears, eyes, whiskers, posture and tail. The signals are read together and in context, because no single signal stands for one fixed emotion.

At a glance

Main rule
Read signals together and in context
Friendly greeting
Often an upright tail with a softly curved tip and a relaxed body
Comfort
Soft narrowed eyes and slow blinking can accompany it
Unease
Can show as a crouched tense body, ears sideways or back, and a closely held tail
Exposed belly
Not automatically an invitation to rub it
Pupils
Change with lighting and can change with arousal

Why signals are read together

A cat's body signals are interpreted together and in context. They are not a fixed code in which one signal equals one emotion.

Pupils are an example. Pupil size changes with lighting and can also change with arousal, so one pupil size does not identify one emotion.

Sources: [1] [2] [6]

Signs of comfort and interest

An upright tail with a softly curved tip, together with a relaxed body, often accompanies a friendly greeting. Soft, narrowed eyes and slow blinking can accompany comfort, and experiments link slow-blink interactions with positive communication between cats and humans.

Ears directed forward and whiskers pointed toward an object can accompany interest or attention. That is not necessarily happiness. A relaxed cat with its belly exposed is not automatically inviting a belly rub.

Sources: [1] [3] [4]

Signs of unease and when to pause

A crouched, tense body, ears turned sideways or back and a tail held close can form a cluster of unease signals.

During contact, body tension, ears turning back and a lashing tail can indicate that the interaction should pause.

Sources: [1] [2] [5]

Cat Atlas / Extraordinary senses · October 15, 2026

Cat Atlas — Extraordinary Senses

A cat senses its surroundings with eyes that work in dim light, mobile outer ears that hear higher frequencies than humans do, a nose that reports on food, places and other animals, and whiskers that register touch at the follicle.

At a glance

Dim-light vision
Rod photoreceptors and the reflective tapetum contribute; this is not vision in total darkness
Hearing
Higher sound frequencies than humans hear
Outer ears
Mobile pinnae help collect and locate sound
Whisker sensing
Receptors associated with the follicle, not nerves inside the hair shaft
Balance
Semicircular canals of the inner ear
Tongue spines
Backward-facing keratin papillae; not taste buds

Eyes and dim light

The cornea and lens direct incoming light to the retina, and the optic nerve carries visual information. The pupil changes size in response to light.

Rod photoreceptors in the retina and the reflective tapetum contribute to vision in dim light. That does not mean a cat can see in total darkness.

Sources: [1] [2]

Ears, hearing and balance

The pinnae, the outer ear flaps, are mobile and help collect and locate sound. The ear canal, the eardrum and the cochlea each have a distinct role in hearing. Cats hear higher sound frequencies than humans.

The semicircular canals are balance structures in the inner ear. They are separate from the cochlea, which is used in hearing.

Sources: [2] [3]

Smell and whiskers

Smell gives a cat information about food, places and other animals. When a whisker is mechanically displaced, the movement stimulates sensory receptors associated with the whisker's follicle. The sensing is not done by nerves inside the hair shaft.

Sources: [2] [4]

Spines on the tongue

The tongue carries backward-facing papillae made of keratin. These visible spines contribute to grooming. They are not taste buds.

Sources: [5]

Cat Atlas — Inside the Cat

A cat's organs work as connected systems. The heart and lungs move blood and exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide, the digestive tract handles food, the urinary system removes wastes, and padded paws carry curved, retractile claws.

At a glance

Subject

Stomach

Organs of the abdomen

The liver lies directly behind the diaphragm, on the side toward the tail. The stomach lies behind the liver, and loops of intestine occupy the abdomen.

Sources: [1]

Heart, lungs and the path of blood

The heart pumps blood, and the lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide. Blood returning from the body enters the right side of the heart and travels to the lungs. It then returns to the left side of the heart, which pumps it out to the body.

Sources: [2]

Digestion and the urinary system

The digestive tract breaks down food, absorbs nutrients and moves the remaining waste toward elimination. The urinary system includes two kidneys, ureters, a bladder and a urethra. It removes wastes and regulates water and electrolytes.

Sources: [3] [4] [5]

Paws and claws

Cats have curved, retractile claws, which means the claws can be drawn back. The claws provide grip. The paws are padded, and the pads cushion contact.

Sources: [6]

Diverticulitis — When a Bowel Pouch Becomes Inflamed

Diverticulitis means that diverticula, pouches that push outward through weak spots in the colon wall, have become inflamed. Most people with diverticula do not develop symptoms or problems.

At a glance

Diverticula
Pouches that push outward through weak spots in the colon wall
Most common location
The sigmoid colon
Diverticulosis
Pouches are present
Diverticulitis
Diverticula become inflamed
Possible symptoms
Severe constant abdominal pain, often in the lower left abdomen, and fever

Pouches in the colon wall

Diverticula are pouches that push outward through weak spots in the colon wall, most often in the sigmoid colon. Diverticulosis means the pouches are present. Most people with diverticula do not develop symptoms or problems. Diverticulitis means the diverticula become inflamed. It is not an inevitable progression of diverticulosis.

Sources: [1] [3]

Symptoms and assessment

Symptoms can include severe, constant abdominal pain, often in the lower left abdomen, and fever. The location is not universal. Assessment may include blood tests and CT imaging to clarify the diagnosis and to distinguish other causes of the symptoms.

Sources: [3]

Care that depends on severity

Treatment depends on severity and on patient factors. Uncomplicated diverticulitis may be managed at home under a clinician's guidance. Treatment may include pain relief selected by a clinician and temporary dietary changes. Antibiotics are not needed for every person.

Severe disease or complications may need hospital treatment, and abscess drainage or surgery can be necessary in selected cases. A perforation of the colon wall or an abscess is a possible complication, not the normal appearance of every case.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Warning signs

Worsening persistent pain, fever, or vomiting that prevents keeping fluids down warrants prompt medical assessment. Severe abdominal pain with vomiting, a swollen abdomen or an inability to pass stool or gas warrants emergency care.

Sources: [3]

After an episode

After the acute episode, fiber intake as advised by a clinician, physical activity and not smoking may lower future risk. Prevention is not guaranteed. The infographic provides general education, not a diagnosis or an individualized treatment plan.

Sources: [2] [3]

Gout — Crystals in the Joint

Gout is inflammatory arthritis in which urate can accumulate and form needle-shaped crystals in joints, commonly the big toe joint, triggering painful inflammation. A flare brings sudden severe pain, warmth and swelling.

At a glance

What it is
Inflammatory arthritis
Crystals
Needle-shaped urate crystals in joints
Joint commonly affected
The big toe joint, though it can affect other joints
A flare
Sudden severe pain, warmth and swelling, sometimes redness
Tests
Blood urate testing and sometimes joint-fluid crystal testing

Where urate comes from

Gout is inflammatory arthritis. Urate can accumulate and form needle-shaped crystals in joints, which triggers painful inflammation. Urate comes from the breakdown of purines in body tissues and in foods, and it normally leaves the body in urine. Too much production or too little removal can raise the level of urate in the blood. Not everyone with high urate develops gout.

Genes, kidney disease, alcohol and some medicines can increase the risk of gout. Gout is not simply a consequence of food choices.

Sources: [1] [2]

What a flare is like

Gout commonly affects the big toe joint, but it can affect other joints. A flare causes sudden severe pain, warmth and swelling. There is sometimes redness, which may be harder to see on darker skin.

Sources: [1] [2]

Evaluation and treatment

First-time symptoms need medical evaluation. Blood urate testing, and sometimes testing of joint fluid for crystals, help evaluate gout. Clinicians treat flares with anti-inflammatory medicines such as NSAIDs or steroids, selected for individual safety. Rest, elevation and a wrapped cold pack can help.

Urate-lowering medicine may be needed for recurrent attacks or high uric acid. The NHS guidance is that it is taken regularly, even when there are no symptoms. Healthy habits support prevention but do not replace needed medicines.

Sources: [2]

When joint infection is possible

A suddenly painful, swollen joint with worsening pain, fever or chills, or feeling sick needs urgent assessment, because joint infection is possible.

Sources: [2]

Peptic Ulcers — A Break in the Digestive Lining

A peptic ulcer is a sore in the lining of the stomach or the duodenum. Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID medicines are the most common causes, and treatment targets the cause.

At a glance

What it is
A sore in the lining of the stomach or duodenum
Most common causes
Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID medicines
Possible symptoms
Upper abdominal burning or discomfort, feeling full early, nausea and bloating
Without symptoms
Some people have no symptoms
Tests
H. pylori breath or stool tests; sometimes upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
Treatment
Antibiotics for H. pylori; acid-reducing medicines such as proton pump inhibitors

Where ulcers form and why

A peptic ulcer is a sore in the lining of the stomach or the duodenum. The two locations are alternatives, and an ulcer is not necessarily present in both at once. Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID medicines are the most common causes. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can make the stomach lining more prone to damage and ulcers. That is a risk, not a universal outcome.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Symptoms

Symptoms can include burning or discomfort in the upper abdomen, feeling full early, nausea and bloating. Some people have no symptoms. Food can relieve pain briefly in some people and worsen it in others, so meal timing cannot diagnose an ulcer.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Testing and treatment

Evaluation may use breath or stool tests for H. pylori and sometimes upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. Treatment targets the cause. It includes antibiotics for H. pylori infection and acid-reducing medicines such as proton pump inhibitors. A clinician may review or change NSAID medicines, and the infographic does not direct anyone to change prescribed medicines independently. Follow-up tests may be needed to confirm that treatment has worked.

Sources: [1] [3]

The place of diet

Diet is not considered an important primary cause of peptic ulcers or an important primary treatment for them. Foods may worsen symptoms for some people, and they do not replace treating H. pylori or medication causes.

Sources: [1] [3]

Complications and warning signs

Ulcers may cause bleeding or perforation. These are possible complications, not present in every ulcer. Vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, black tarry stool, sudden severe persistent abdominal pain or fainting needs urgent or emergency assessment. The infographic provides general education, not a diagnosis or an individualized treatment plan.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Pneumonia — When Air Sacs Fill

Pneumonia is an infection of one or both lungs in which the alveoli, the air sacs, can fill with fluid or pus. Bacteria and viruses commonly cause it, and treatment depends on the cause and the severity.

At a glance

What it is
An infection of one or both lungs
Air sacs
Alveoli can fill with fluid or pus
Causes
Commonly bacteria and viruses; fungi can also cause it
Possible symptoms
Cough, fever, chills, shortness of breath, chest pain and tiredness
Higher risk

Infection in the air sacs

Pneumonia is an infection of one or both lungs. The alveoli are air sacs that can fill with fluid or pus. Bacteria and viruses commonly cause pneumonia, and fungi can also cause it. Young children, older adults, and people with weakened immunity or chronic lung disease have a higher risk.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Symptoms and assessment

Symptoms may include cough, fever, chills, shortness of breath, chest pain and tiredness, and they vary. Clinical assessment may include a chest examination, a chest X-ray and blood tests. Symptoms alone do not establish the diagnosis.

Sources: [1] [2]

Treatment depends on the cause

Bacterial pneumonia is usually treated with antibiotics. Treatment depends on the cause and the severity, so antibiotics are not a universal treatment. Rest and fluids support recovery, and severe illness may require hospital care and oxygen.

Sources: [1] [2]

Warning signs and risk reduction

Severe trouble breathing, blue or pale lips or skin, sudden confusion, or coughing blood require emergency care. Worsening symptoms need prompt medical assessment.

Recommended vaccines can prevent some of the infections that cause pneumonia. Handwashing and not smoking help reduce the risk.

Sources: [1] [2]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Type 1 Diabetes — The Missing Insulin Signal

Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which immune activity destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. With little or no insulin, blood glucose rises, and insulin treatment is essential.

At a glance

Kind of disease
Autoimmune
What is destroyed
Insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas
Age
Can develop at any age
Common symptoms
Frequent urination, thirst, fatigue, unexplained weight loss and blurred vision
Essential treatment
Insulin
Medical emergency
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)

The missing insulin signal

Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease. Immune activity destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas, which causes little or no insulin. Insulin helps glucose enter the body's cells for energy, and insufficient insulin causes blood glucose to rise. The tissue and glucose symbols in the infographic are schematic and not to scale. Type 1 diabetes can develop at any age, and a family history raises the risk.

Sources: [1] [2]

Symptoms and diagnosis

Common symptoms include frequent urination, thirst, fatigue, unexplained weight loss and blurred vision. Suspected type 1 diabetes needs urgent medical assessment. Diagnosis uses blood glucose tests, and autoantibody tests help establish the type.

Sources: [1] [2]

Insulin and monitoring

Insulin treatment is essential. Insulin pens or pumps and regular glucose monitoring support individualized care with a diabetes team. Healthy eating and activity support management, but they do not replace insulin. Too much insulin can cause low blood glucose, so treatment and monitoring require an individualized care plan.

Sources: [1]

Diabetic ketoacidosis

Without enough insulin, the breakdown of fat produces ketones. These can accumulate and cause diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a medical emergency. Vomiting or abdominal pain, fast deep breathing, fruity breath, sleepiness or confusion may signal DKA. The guidance for these signs is to seek emergency care immediately, especially when they come with thirst and frequent urination.

Sources: [1] [2]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Cat Claws — The Pivot Beneath the Fur

A domestic cat's claw is pushed out when the deep digital flexor pulls on the last bone of the toe, and elastic ligaments draw it back when it is not in use. Superficial horn caps can shed from the claw, which keeps the tip sharp.

At a glance

Shown
Normal domestic cat forepaw, digits 2 to 5
Joint involved
Distal interphalangeal joint, between the middle and distal phalanges
Pushes the claw out
Contraction of the deep digital flexor
Pulls the claw back
Elastic ligaments, passively; the lateral one is the most important
What is shed
Superficial horn caps, not the entire claw or the toe bone

The bones and the sheath

The infographic shows the mechanism in a normal forepaw of a domestic cat, in digits 2 to 5. In each of these toes the middle phalanx and the distal phalanx, the last bone of the toe, form the distal interphalangeal joint.

The cornified claw sheath surrounds living tissues that are supported by the distal phalanx. The horny sheath is not the same thing as the bone.

Sources: [1] [2]

Pushing the claw out

Protrusion is active. The deep digital flexor attaches to the flexor process of the distal phalanx, and when it contracts it protrudes the claw. The digital extensors stabilize the joints nearer the body.

Sources: [1]

Drawing the claw back

Retraction is passive. Elastic ligaments retract the claw, and the lateral elastic ligament is the most important of them. The distal phalanx does not telescope straight into the toe. It comes to overlap the middle phalanx.

Retraction protects the claw from wear when it is not in use. The retracted claw is sheltered in a protective fold of skin.

Sources: [1] [2]

Shedding the horn caps

Superficial caps of horn can shed without injury to the living tissues underneath. This keeps the tips sharp. A shed cap is not the entire claw, and it is not the toe bone.

Sources: [2]

Colorpoints — Pigment Meets Temperature

In Siamese-type colorpoint cats, the cooler extremities have darker fur and the warmer body has lighter fur. The pattern is associated with variants in TYR, and pigment production in these cats is temperature-sensitive.

At a glance

Gene
TYR, which encodes the enzyme tyrosinase
Enzyme's role
Initial steps of melanin pigment synthesis
Darker fur
Cooler extremities: face, ears, paws and tail
Lighter fur
Warmer body regions
Inheritance
Siamese-type allele is recessive to the full-color wild-type allele

Pigment that depends on temperature

In the Siamese-type pattern, the cooler extremities have darker fur and the warmer regions of the body have lighter fur, because pigment production is temperature-sensitive. The infographic marks the face, ears, paws and tail as the points.

This is a mechanism of pigment production, not a stain on the surface of the fur. The warm and cool regions in the infographic are schematic. They carry no numerical temperatures and are not an actual thermal scan.

Sources: [1] [2]

The gene involved

Variants in TYR are associated with Siamese-type colorpoint pigmentation. TYR encodes tyrosinase, an enzyme involved in the initial steps of melanin pigment synthesis.

The Siamese-type allele is recessive to the full-color wild-type allele. Cats with two copies can express the pointed pattern. Other genetic loci also influence how a coat looks.

Sources: [1] [2]

Not the same as albinism

Different TYR variants are associated with Siamese and Burmese pigmentation, and a distinct TYR variant is associated with complete albinism. The point pattern is not the same as a complete absence of pigment.

Sources: [1] [2]

Kneading — A Familiar Rhythm, an Uncertain Motive

Kneading is a paw-pressing behavior related to nursing that can persist into adult life. What it means in an adult cat is a matter of interpretation, not certainty.

What is established

Kneading is a paw-pressing behavior related to nursing. Nursing kittens knead their mother's belly, which helps stimulate milk flow. The behavior can persist into adult life.

The infographic shows it as alternating presses of the forepaws on a soft blanket. This is kneading, not walking or scratching. Some cats knead while purring.

Sources: [1] [2]

What remains interpretation

Kneading can be a sign of affection, but it is not a guaranteed reading of a cat's thoughts. The cat's broader engagement and the context matter. No one can get inside a cat's mind, so an adult cat's motive for kneading is an interpretation and not a certainty.

Purring does not settle the question. It occurs in contented cats and in stressed cats, so purring alone does not prove happiness.
