Tail Signals — Read the Whole Cat

A cat's tail is read together with its ears, its posture and the situation it is in. A single tail pose is not a guaranteed emotion or a diagnosis.

At a glance

Main rule
Read the tail with ear positions, posture and interaction context
Tail up
Can be a friendly greeting, particularly between cats and humans
Tucked tail
With a low crouch and flattened ears, can indicate fear
Lashing tail
With ears moving backward during petting, can precede aggression
Raised tail fur

Ears and tails

Reading the tail in context

Tails are interpreted together with ear positions, posture and the context of the interaction. A single pose is not a guaranteed emotion or a diagnosis.

In an observational study of cats at a shelter, ear positions were more predictive than tails of how an interaction between cats turned out. The study's exact frequencies should not be generalized, and the finding does not make tails meaningless.

Sources: [1] [2]

Tail up and tail tucked

A cat that approaches with its tail up can be giving a friendly greeting, particularly in interactions between cats and humans. The friendly version shown in the infographic has smooth fur, upright ears and an easy walking posture. A raised tail is not a universal invitation to touch.

A tucked tail combined with a low crouch and flattened ears can indicate fear. These cues occur as a cluster, and they are not a certainty.

Sources: [1] [2]

Lashing and raised fur

During petting, a lashing tail with ears moving backward can come before aggression. Cornell's veterinary guidance is to stop petting and allow a pause with no contact. Tail movement can also occur in play, so context matters.

Raised tail fur with an arched back and ears flattened back can accompany defensive or aggressive displays. A puffed tail does not stand for one unique emotion.

Taurine — An Essential Dietary Link

Cats need taurine in their diet because they have only a very limited ability to make it themselves. Taurine deficiency can cause central retinal degeneration and dilated cardiomyopathy.

At a glance

Why diet matters
Cats have a very limited ability to synthesize taurine from cysteine
Dietary source
Animal-source foodstuffs
Deficiency can cause
Central retinal degeneration and dilated cardiomyopathy
Food label statement
Nutritional adequacy: complete and balanced for the appropriate life stage
Supplements

Why cats cannot make enough

Cats have a very limited ability to synthesize taurine from cysteine, so taurine in the diet is essential. Low activities of cysteine dioxygenase and cysteinesulfinic acid decarboxylase limit how much taurine a cat makes.

The infographic simplifies this to a limited internal supply. It does not mean cats make no taurine at all.

Sources: [2]

What deficiency can do

Taurine deficiency can cause central retinal degeneration, in the eye, and dilated cardiomyopathy, in the heart muscle. The infographic uses the eye and the heart to illustrate why adequate dietary taurine matters. It does not diagnose disease or describe treatment.

Sources: [2]

Taurine and the whole diet

Animal-source foodstuffs supply taurine. A meat ingredient alone does not establish that a diet is complete. Cats are obligate carnivores, and they require a balance of multiple nutrients, not taurine alone.

Cornell's feeding guidance is to choose cat food with a nutritional adequacy statement that indicates complete and balanced nutrition for the appropriate life stage. Ingredients and nutrient balance are distinct things. Supplements are usually unnecessary with a complete, balanced diet and should not be given without veterinary approval.

Sources: [1] [2]

Whiskers — Touch Before the Muzzle Arrives

A cat's whisker senses by physical contact. When the shaft bends against an object, the mechanical deformation reaches the follicle at the base of the whisker, where sensory receptors are activated.

From contact to nerve signal

Whiskers give a cat tactile contact with its surroundings. In the infographic, a whisker touches an object before the muzzle reaches it. This is sensing through physical contact, not remote sensing without physical input.

Contact bends the whisker shaft, and the mechanical deformation reaches the follicle, where it activates sensory receptors. In the cat, movement of the maxillary whiskers evokes impulses in sensory fibers of the infraorbital nerve.

Sources: [1] [2]

Where the receptors are

The sensory receptors are at the base of the whisker, within the follicle. They are not distributed along the exposed shaft.

Sources: [2]

Slow and rapid responses

The sensory fibers serving cat whiskers include slowly adapting responses, which are to a displacement that is maintained, and rapidly adapting responses, which are to whisker movement. The traces in the diagram are qualitative. They carry no measured scales.

Sources: [1]

Limits of the diagram

The cutaway of the follicle is a simplified schematic and is not to scale. The Northwestern University whisker simulation used data from rats, so it does not demonstrate that a particular S-shaped bend inside the follicle occurs in cats.

Balloon Fear — Anticipating the Pop

Fear of balloons is a descriptive label, not a separate diagnostic category. Fear of balloons and noise, with avoidance, has been documented in a published case report. The rest of the picture comes from evidence about specific phobias in general.

At a glance

Status
A descriptive fear label, not a separate diagnostic category
Documented in

Dislike, startle and phobia

A phobia involves intense fear that is out of proportion to actual danger. An ordinary dislike or startle is not by itself a diagnosis. Fear of balloons is used here as a descriptive fear label, not as a separate diagnostic category.

Sources: [1] [4]

What one case report documents

For some people, balloons and the prospect of a pop are feared cues. A published case report described a fear of balloons and noise, with avoidance of situations where balloons might be encountered. That is a single case. It is an example, not a trigger profile that applies to everyone, and it is not proof of a balloon-specific treatment effect.

Sources: [3]

Anticipation, alarm and avoidance

Thinking about a feared object can provoke anxiety before an encounter. Phobic anxiety can include a racing heartbeat, shaking and sweating. The alarm can exceed the actual danger presented, and the fear is real even when it is disproportionate. The imagined pop is an anticipation, not an explosion that is happening.

Fear can lead a person to avoid situations where the object may be encountered, and avoidance can interfere with social life. The infographic shows someone missing a gathering as an example of this general pattern. It makes no statement about how common that is.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [4]

Treatment evidence is general

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and exposure-based therapy are evidence-based approaches for specific phobias generally, and exposure treatment can progress gradually. That general evidence is not a guarantee of a cure for balloon fear.

A health professional is relevant when fear affects daily life. A provider can assess symptoms and guide treatment. The infographic is educational, not an individual treatment plan.

Sources: [1] [2] [4]

Bridge Fear — Crossing and Anticipation

Bridge fear is a descriptive label for fear of bridges, not a separate diagnosis. It is explained here through the general pattern of phobias about places or situations: anticipation, body alarm and avoidance.

At a glance

A descriptive fear label, not a separate diagnosis

A label, not a diagnosis

Bridge fear is used here as a descriptive fear label, not as a separate diagnosis. Persistent situational fear that is excessive and interferes with life warrants assessment, and diagnosis requires professional assessment. Educational artwork is not a diagnosis.

Sources: [1] [2]

Anxiety before, fear during

Phobias may concern places or situations. Contact with the feared situation, or even thinking about it, can cause anxiety. The infographic shows approaching a bridge, crossing it and imagining a crossing as examples of that general principle. It does not claim that every person has these triggers.

Anxiety anticipates a future concern, while fear responds to an immediate threat. Fear can involve a fight-or-flight response. Possible body symptoms include a racing heart, trembling, dizziness and muscle tension. These are possibilities, not symptoms everyone has.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Alarm is not a safety reading

Clinically significant anxiety is out of proportion to the situation. Feeling intense alarm is not, on its own, evidence that the illustrated bridge is dangerous. Ordinary safety precautions for the situation still apply, and no guarantee is made about the safety of any bridge.

Avoiding feared situations can limit everyday activities. The detour in the infographic represents that cost. It is not a prescribed coping strategy.

Sources: [2] [3]

Help for situational fear

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can help people identify unhelpful thought patterns and gradually face feared situations. Gradual exposure is an established approach to simple phobias. Care is individualized with a qualified clinician.

The infographic offers no bridge-crossing exercise to do independently and no instruction to enter unsafe situations. The sources advise consulting a health professional when fear affects everyday life.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Choking Phobia — The Meal That Feels Unsafe

Choking phobia, also called phagophobia, is an intense fear of choking with avoidance of swallowing food, drinks or pills. Swallowing difficulty must be medically evaluated, not assumed to be anxiety.

At a glance

Also called
Phagophobia
Core fear
Choking, with avoidance of swallowing food, drinks or pills
Classification

Possible triggers

What choking phobia is

Choking phobia, also called phagophobia, involves an intense fear of choking and avoidance of swallowing food, drinks or pills. It may be classified as a specific phobia. It may follow a frightening choking experience, but it can also arise without one. Education about it does not diagnose an individual.

Sources: [1] [3]

Alarm at mealtimes

Anticipating swallowing, or seeing a meal, can trigger anxiety. Palpitations, trembling and nausea can accompany phobic alarm. Fear of swallowing can lead to avoidance or restriction, which maintains the fear cycle. Severe restriction can cause weight loss and social disruption.

Sources: [1] [2]

Why medical assessment matters

Fear is not proof of an airway blockage. Equally, swallowing difficulty must be medically evaluated, not assumed to be anxiety. Difficulty swallowing, coughing or choking during meals, food feeling stuck, or a wet voice after swallowing warrant urgent medical advice. Assessment may involve a swallowing specialist and a dietitian. Care should protect swallowing safety and nutrition.

Sources: [1] [3]

What is known about treatment

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a treatment for phobias. Behavior therapy, including gradual exposure guided by a clinician, has been reported to help choking phobia. Research on this particular disorder is limited, and it does not justify promises of a cure.

Exposure that involves swallowing is for a clinician to guide after medical assessment. It is not something to attempt as a do-it-yourself food challenge.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Driving Fear — Alarm Behind the Wheel

Driving fear can involve intense fear and avoidance of driving. Specific phobia is one possible clinical explanation, but post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and other presentations also occur.

More than one possible explanation

Driving fear can involve intense fear and avoidance of driving. Specific phobia is one possible clinical explanation. PTSD and other presentations also occur, and professional assessment can distinguish specific phobia from trauma-related symptoms.

In a phobia, fear is out of proportion to actual danger. That does not mean driving is risk-free.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Worry, body alarm and avoided routes

Anticipating a feared situation can cause excessive worry. Body alarm can include a racing or noticeable heartbeat, trembling and dizziness.

People with driving fear may avoid highways and unfamiliar routes. Anxiety and avoidance can restrict driving in general or only particular routes. These are characteristic responses, not a prediction of a crash.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Treatment and how strong the evidence is

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an established treatment for phobias, and exposure is a particularly effective CBT method for phobias generally. Care for driving fear can use professional assessment and an individually planned anxiety hierarchy. Simulator exposure has promising but limited evidence from a pilot study. It is not a guaranteed cure.

Treatment guided by a clinician is not a directive to practice alone in traffic or to ignore road hazards. The driving study cited used assessment and professionally supervised driving. A clinician is the relevant contact when symptoms affect life.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Frog Fear — A Startle in the Reeds

Fear of frogs is a descriptive label, not a separate established diagnostic category. Fears of animals can fall within specific phobia when they are persistent, disproportionate and impairing, and a clinician assesses diagnosis.

At a glance

Status
A descriptive fear label, not a separate established diagnostic category

Where frog fear fits

Fear of frogs is used here as a descriptive fear label. It is not a separate established diagnostic category. Animal-related fears can fall within specific phobia when they are persistent, disproportionate and impairing, and a clinician assesses diagnosis.

The frog encounter in the infographic is illustrative. It stands for the general framework of animal-related specific phobia, not for a separately validated frog-specific diagnosis or treatment. This is general education, not a diagnosis.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Triggers and the body's response

Seeing or anticipating the feared animal, and sometimes just thinking about it, can trigger anxiety. The infographic uses a frog encounter and an anticipated park visit as examples. They are not triggers shared by everyone with this fear.

Body alarm can include a rapid heartbeat, shaking and tense muscles. Fear is associated with a fight-or-flight response.

Phobic fear can be out of proportion to actual danger. The intensity of alarm is not itself evidence of danger, and the risk in the actual setting still matters.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

What avoidance does

Avoidance may reduce anxiety quickly. It can also maintain fear, because it prevents opportunities to revise beliefs and learn coping. Avoiding places may interfere with everyday life.

Sources: [3]

Help in small steps

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can help people examine unhelpful thoughts and gradually face feared situations. Graded exposure uses small, manageable steps. A qualified professional can help tailor treatment.

The infographic is not an instruction to handle wildlife or to force exposure. Professional help is relevant if fear or avoidance affects everyday life.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Blushing, sweating, trembling, rapid heartbeat, nausea, mind going blank; responses differ

CBT with a therapist

More than shyness

Social anxiety disorder, also called social phobia, is a persistent, overwhelming fear of social situations that involve possible scrutiny, negative judgment, humiliation or rejection. It is more than ordinary shyness, and it can impair daily life.

An educational chart is not a diagnosis. Professional assessment is relevant when anxiety disrupts school, work, relationships or daily life.

Sources: [1] [2]

Triggers and symptoms

Possible triggers include meeting new people, speaking publicly and eating while others are present. Some people have anxiety mainly during performance. Worry can occur before a social event, and a self-critical review can follow afterward.

Symptoms may include blushing, sweating, trembling, a rapid heartbeat, nausea and the mind going blank. Responses differ among people.

Sources: [1] [2]

Feared judgment and avoidance

Fearful predictions that other people are judging or rejecting a person may be distorted or untrue. Anxiety is not proof that rejection is occurring. Avoiding feared social situations can feel helpful briefly, but anxiety is likely to remain without treatment.

Sources: [1]

Treatment with a clinician

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with a therapist is a well-supported treatment. It addresses patterns of thinking and behavior. Graduated exposure is a CBT method that progressively approaches feared activities. Treatment is tailored with a clinician. Medication such as an SSRI may also help some people.

Sources: [1] [2]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Cave Pearls — Stone Grown Around a Grain

Cave pearls are mineral concretions with concentric bands that form in shallow cave pools. Carbonate is deposited in successive layers around a particle such as a grain of sand.

At a glance

What they are
Concentrically banded mineral concretions
Where they form
Shallow cave pools
Nucleus
A particle, such as a grain of sand
Water supply
Water dripping from above or slowly flowing into the pool
Shape
Varies; some are rounded and others irregular

How a pearl grows

Cave pearls form in shallow cave pools. Water dripping from above or slowly flowing into the pool supplies the dissolved material. The loss of carbon dioxide to the cave air promotes the precipitation of carbonate around particles in the pool. A grain of sand can act as the nucleus, and successive mineral deposits form concentric bands around it.

Excess carbonate precipitate can coat the floor of the pool and build cups or nests around the pearls.

Sources: [1] [2]

Inside a pearl

A cross section of a cave pearl can show crystals arranged radially outward from a central nucleus. The calcite texture drawn in the infographic is a generalized schematic.

Sources: [2]

Why some are round

Cave pearls vary in shape. Some are rounded and others are irregular. In the National Park Service explanation, roundness results from the outer layer growing in all directions in supersaturated water, not from polishing by rotation. Dripping water can agitate cave pearls, but agitation is not the same as tumbling them smooth.

Coral Bleaching — The Partnership Comes Apart

Reef-building corals depend on microscopic algae that live in their tissue and provide much of their color and food. Stress such as heat can disrupt the partnership and turn the coral white, which leaves it vulnerable but not necessarily dead.

At a glance

Coral
An animal colony of tiny tentacled polyps on a hard skeleton
Partner
Microscopic symbiotic algae called zooxanthellae
What the algae provide
Much of the coral's color and a major food source
What the coral provides
A place to live
Cause of bleaching
Heat stress, though not only warm-water stress
Outcome
Recovery is possible if stress eases and algae return

Coral and algae together

A reef-building coral is an animal. It is a colony of tiny polyps with tentacles that build a hard skeleton and cover it. Microscopic symbiotic algae called zooxanthellae live within the coral's tissue. They provide much of its color and a major source of its food.

The algae use sunlight, carbon dioxide and water for photosynthesis. Much of the food they produce feeds the coral, and the coral provides the algae with a place to live.

Sources: [1] [2]

What happens in bleaching

Heat stress can disrupt the partnership and cause the coral to lose its algae, their coloration, or both. Bleaching is not limited to stress from warm water. When the algae and their pigments are lost, the white skeleton becomes visible through the living coral tissue, which is nearly transparent.

Sources: [1] [2]

After bleaching

Bleached coral is not necessarily dead. It has lost a major source of food and is vulnerable. Recovery is possible if the stress eases and the algae return. Prolonged stress and loss of algae can lead to death.

Sources: [1] [2]

Eyed Click Beetle — False Eyes and a Loaded Hinge

The eyed click beetle is a long black beetle mottled with white scales, with large false eyespots behind its head. Its larvae hunt other beetle larvae in decaying hardwood, and click beetles in general can jump using a hinge in the thorax.

At a glance

Scientific name
Alaus oculatus
Family
Elateridae
Adult length
About 1 to 1 3/4 inches
Range
Eastern United States and southern Ontario and Quebec
Habitat
Wooded habitats associated with hardwoods
Larval prey
Wood-boring beetle larvae in decaying hardwood

False eyes and true eyes

The eyed click beetle, Alaus oculatus, belongs to the family Elateridae. The adult has an elongated black body mottled with white, six legs, antennae and paired wing covers. Minute scales form the mottled surface pattern. Adults are about 1 to 1 3/4 inches long.

Large black eyespots ringed with white sit on the prothorax, behind the head. They are not eyes. The true eyes are much smaller and are on the head.

Sources: [1] [2]

Larvae in decaying hardwood

The species occurs in the eastern United States and in southern Ontario and Quebec, in wooded habitats associated with hardwoods. Its larvae prey on the larvae of wood-boring beetles in decaying hardwood, including rotting oak, cherry and apple stumps.

The larvae are hardened and yellowish to dark brown, with a nearly black head and dark segments at the end of the abdomen. The upper side of the last abdominal segment has conical bumps and paired forked teeth. The larva and the adult are the documented forms. No duration or in-between form is given.

Sources: [1] [2]

How click beetles click and jump

The jump is described for click beetles in general. A hinge in the thorax, behind the head, allows jumping without a leg-powered takeoff. A peg holds against a lip while soft tissue deforms. On release, elastic recoil causes rapid unbending and an audible click.

The infographic's diagram of this hinge is a schematic for the click beetle family. It is not the measured internal geometry of the eyed click beetle.

Sources: [3]

Ferrofluid — A Liquid Shaped by Fields

A ferrofluid is a liquid that carries tiny magnetic solid particles in suspension. In a strong enough magnetic field, its flat surface rises into spikes oriented along the field.

At a glance

What it is
Tiny magnetic solid particles suspended in a liquid carrier
Example particles
Magnetite (Fe3O4) nanoparticles
Example coating
Oleic-acid surfactant
Example carrier
Oil
Spike effect
Normal-field instability, also called Rosensweig instability
Spike pattern
May have a hexagonal arrangement

What is in the liquid

Ferrofluid contains tiny magnetic solid particles suspended in a liquid carrier. One example is an oil-based magnetite ferrofluid, which can contain nanoparticles of magnetite (Fe3O4) coated with an oleic-acid surfactant, in oil.

The polar heads of the surfactant attach to the magnetite surfaces, and its hydrocarbon tails extend into the oil. The coating helps keep the particles apart and prevents clumping.

Sources: [1] [2]

Why spikes form

A magnet beneath a shallow dish can cause the surface of the ferrofluid to rise into spikes oriented along the magnetic field. The effect is the normal-field instability, also called the Rosensweig instability.

In a sufficiently strong vertical magnetic field, magnetic effects overcome the stabilizing effects of gravity and surface tension, and the flat surface develops spikes. A regular pattern of spikes may have a hexagonal arrangement.

Sources: [1] [2]

What the drawing simplifies

The field lines and enlarged particles in the infographic are explanatory schematics. They are not visible structures, and they do not share one physical scale.

Sources: [1] [2]

Meadow Spittlebug — A Nymph Inside a Bubble Shelter

The meadow spittlebug is a sap-feeding bug whose nymphs turn excess xylem sap into a shelter of foam. The foam hides the nymph from predators, buffers temperature extremes and helps keep it from drying out.

At a glance

Scientific name
Philaenus spumarius
Adult's other name
Froghopper
Food
Xylem sap of many herbaceous plants, including clover and strawberries
Nymph color
Pale green or yellow
Adult color
Generally tan to brown or gray
Adult size
Under a quarter inch long

Nymph and adult

The meadow spittlebug, Philaenus spumarius, is a hemipteran, and its adult is also called a froghopper. The nymphs are pale green or yellow, and lime-green nymphs can have red eyes. Adults are generally tan to brown or gray. Adult spittlebugs are tiny, under a quarter inch long, and hop between plants.

Like other insects, it has six legs and a distinct head, thorax and abdomen. The small nymphs are wingless and the adults are winged. The meadow spittlebug occurs in the North American Midwest and feeds on many herbaceous plants, including clover and strawberries.

Sources: [1] [2] [4]

A diet of xylem sap

Both adults and nymphs feed on xylem sap, the sap that carries water through the plant. Its nutrient concentration is low, so the insects have to process large quantities. The piercing and sucking mouthparts of hemipterans extend below the head, and in hoppers the proboscis points down and back. The infographic's simplified feeding study shows the mouthparts reaching the plant's sap tissues.

The internal view of the gut is generalized. Insects in general have a tube-like alimentary canal that runs from mouth to anus, with a foregut, midgut and hindgut. Nutrient absorption in the midgut is a general function. The cutaway is not a measured dissection of this species.

Sources: [1] [3] [4]

How the foam is made

Nymphs feed head downward and excrete the excess sap through the anus, not the mouth. Air is mixed with the excreted fluid as movements of the abdomen form bubbles, and secretions from epidermal glands stabilize the foam. The nymph uses its legs to pull the forming bubbles forward over its body.

The foam conceals nymphs from predators, buffers temperature extremes and helps prevent drying. It is protective, but it is not an invulnerable shield.

Sources: [1] [2]

A life cycle without a pupa

In the temperate life cycle described, eggs overwinter in plant stems. Nymphs hatch in spring, molt as they grow and become winged adults. Females lay eggs in late summer to fall. Hemipterans have incomplete metamorphosis, with no pupal stage.

Sources: [1] [4]

Water Scorpion — Breathing Through a Tail Tube

The water scorpion is a flattened freshwater bug, not a true scorpion. It ambushes prey among submerged plants and dead leaves and breathes air from above the surface through a long tube at its rear.

At a glance

Scientific name
Nepa cinerea
Group
Hemiptera, family Nepidae
Body length
About 20 mm, not counting the breathing tube
Habitat
Near bank vegetation, over mud or clay
Prey
Aquatic insects and small animals, including tadpoles

A tail tube for breathing

The water scorpion, Nepa cinerea, is an insect in the order Hemiptera and the family Nepidae. It is not a true scorpion. The long breathing siphon at its rear is made of two half-tubes that fit together. It conducts atmospheric air from above the water surface to the respiratory system. It is not a stinger.

The internal breathing anatomy in the infographic is generalized. In insects in general, openings called spiracles admit air to branching tracheal tubes and finer tracheoles. Oxygen diffuses to the tissues and carbon dioxide diffuses out. The infographic combines the water scorpion's siphon with this general tracheal network. It is a simplified schematic, not a dissection of the species, and it gives no exact spiracle positions for Nepa cinerea.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [4]

An ambush hunter

The water scorpion's flattened body hides among submerged vegetation and dead leaves. From there it ambushes aquatic insects and small animals, including tadpoles. Its raptorial front legs fold over the prey and grip it, and its sharp proboscis draws up the internal fluids. The other two pairs of legs are used to crawl along the bottom.

Sources: [1] [2]

Wings, eggs and nymphs

The adult has two pairs of wings: protective front wings and membranous hindwings. The hindwings permit flight between watery habitats. Eggs are laid in vegetation just below the water surface. The nymphs look like wingless adults and develop through molts to adulthood. No pupal stage is shown.

Sources: [1]

Size and where it is found

The body is approximately 20 mm long, not counting the breathing tube. The water scorpion lives near bank vegetation over mud or clay. The species occurs in Britain. In Norway it is recorded in the southeast and along the coast north to Bergen.

Sources: [1] [2] [4]

Atrial Fibrillation — An Irregular Rhythm

Atrial fibrillation (AFib) is an irregular heart rhythm in which the upper chambers beat irregularly and do not work with the lower chambers as they should. Blood may pool and form clots, and a possible complication is ischemic stroke.

At a glance

What it is
An irregular heart rhythm
Chambers
Two upper chambers, the atria; two lower chambers, the ventricles
Possible symptoms
Palpitations, fatigue, shortness of breath and lightheadedness, or no symptoms
Possible complication
A clot that blocks an artery supplying the brain, causing ischemic stroke
Diagnosis
Clinician assessment and an electrocardiogram (ECG/EKG)

An uncoordinated rhythm

Atrial fibrillation, or AFib, is an irregular heart rhythm. The two upper chambers of the heart are the atria, and the two lower chambers are the ventricles. In AFib the atria beat irregularly, and the atria and ventricles do not work together as they should. That reduces the efficient flow of blood from the atria to the ventricles.

Sources: [1] [2]

Clots and stroke

Blood may pool and form clots in the heart. The left atrial appendage is a small sac in the wall of the left atrium where clots can form. A clot can travel to an artery that supplies the brain and block it, causing an ischemic stroke. This is a possible complication, not an inevitable one.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [6]

Symptoms, risk factors and diagnosis

AFib may cause fluttering or pounding palpitations, fatigue, shortness of breath and lightheadedness, or it may cause no symptoms. Risk increases with age. High blood pressure, sleep apnea and excess alcohol are among the risk factors, and there is not a single universal cause. Clinician assessment and an electrocardiogram (ECG or EKG) diagnose AFib. Longer monitoring may detect intermittent episodes.

Sources: [1] [2] [4] [5]

Individualized management

Management can include heart-rate control, rhythm control with medicines, electrical cardioversion or catheter ablation in selected people, and management of underlying risk factors. Treatment is individualized. Treating high blood pressure and sleep apnea, and discussing alcohol use with a clinician, are relevant elements of AFib care.

Anticoagulants may lower the risk of stroke when they are indicated after clinical assessment, but they carry a risk of bleeding. Rhythm treatment does not mean that assessment of stroke risk can be ignored.

Sources: [3] [6]

Emergency signs

The guidance is to call 911 immediately for sudden weakness or trouble speaking, or for chest pressure that lasts minutes or returns. These can indicate a stroke or a heart attack and are not to be dismissed as routine AFib symptoms.

Sources: [6]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Celiac Disease — The Intestinal Surface

Celiac disease is an autoimmune condition in which eating gluten triggers an abnormal immune reaction that damages the small intestine. It is managed with a lifelong gluten-free diet, which is not a cure.

At a glance

Type of condition
Autoimmune
Trigger
Gluten, which occurs in wheat, barley and rye
Organ affected
Small intestine
Evaluation
Commonly antibody blood tests and a small-intestinal biopsy
Treatment
Lifelong gluten-free diet with dietitian support

What happens in the intestine

Celiac disease is an autoimmune condition. Eating gluten, which occurs in wheat, barley and rye, triggers an abnormal immune reaction that damages the small intestine. Villi are projections of the small-intestinal lining that increase its surface area. Inflammation and damage can flatten them and impair the absorption of nutrients.

The infographic compares normal villi with villi damaged by celiac disease. The two are schematic comparisons, not before-and-after images from a patient. Poor absorption of nutrients can lead to iron-deficiency anemia and weakening of the bones.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [4]

Symptoms and who gets it

Symptoms may include bloating, abdominal pain, diarrhea and fatigue. Some people have no symptoms. Celiac disease has a genetic susceptibility, and the risk is increased in close relatives. Eating gluten alone does not mean someone will develop it. Celiac disease differs from wheat allergy and from non-celiac gluten sensitivity.

Sources: [1] [2]

Testing before changing the diet

Evaluation commonly uses antibody blood tests and a biopsy of the small intestine. Symptoms alone do not diagnose celiac disease. Starting a gluten-free diet before diagnostic testing can affect the results, so the guidance is not to start one before testing without medical advice.

Sources: [1]

Living with a gluten-free diet

Treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet with support from a dietitian. For most people it improves symptoms and allows the intestine to heal, but it is not a cure.

The management guidance covers reading food labels, avoiding hidden gluten, and following up with a clinician to assess symptoms and nutritional deficiencies, with supplements only if needed. Symptoms that persist despite a gluten-free diet warrant clinical reassessment.

Sources: [1] [2] [4]

General warning signs

The infographic also gives general warning signs that go with diarrhea or vomiting. Being unable to keep fluids down, or having bloody diarrhea, requires urgent advice. Sudden severe abdominal pain requires emergency care. These are general warning signs, not signs that diagnose celiac disease.

Sources: [5]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Hypothyroidism — A Slower Thyroid Signal

Hypothyroidism means the thyroid does not make enough thyroid hormones to meet the body's needs. Low hormone levels slow many body functions, and the missing hormone is replaced with levothyroxine under a clinician's guidance.

At a glance

The gland
Butterfly-shaped, in the lower front of the neck
Most common cause
Hashimoto autoimmune disease
Blood tests
TSH and free T4
Treatment
Levothyroxine, with clinician-guided dosing
Follow-up blood tests
Commonly 6 to 8 weeks after starting or changing a dose

The thyroid and its hormones

The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland in the lower front of the neck. It releases thyroid hormones into the blood to reach the body's tissues. These hormones help regulate energy use and warmth, and they support the brain, heart, muscles and other organs. Hypothyroidism means the thyroid does not make enough of them to meet the body's needs. Low levels slow many body functions.

The pituitary releases TSH, which signals the thyroid to work. In primary thyroid failure, TSH usually rises as hormone output falls. Pituitary disease is an exception.

Sources: [1] [2]

Causes and symptoms

Hashimoto autoimmune disease attacks the thyroid and is the most common cause of hypothyroidism. Thyroid surgery, radiation and some medicines are other causes.

Possible symptoms include fatigue, feeling cold, dry skin, constipation and a slowed heart rate. Symptoms vary, and they do not diagnose hypothyroidism alone.

Sources: [1] [2]

Testing and treatment

TSH and free T4 blood tests help diagnose hypothyroidism. History and examination help find the cause. Levothyroxine replaces the missing thyroid hormone. A clinician guides the dose and follow-up blood tests, which commonly come 6 to 8 weeks after starting or changing a dose. The guidance is not to stop thyroid medicine or change its dose without consulting the clinician.

Sources: [1] [2]

Iodine, pregnancy and a rare emergency

Excess iodine, including kelp or iodine supplements, can worsen autoimmune thyroid disease. Supplements are not a universal fix.

Pregnancy is a reason to contact the clinician promptly, because thyroid hormone needs may change and untreated hypothyroidism can harm mother and baby. In rare cases, severe untreated hypothyroidism can progress to myxedema coma, which is life-threatening and requires immediate medical treatment.

Sources: [1] [2]

Osteoporosis — When the Inner Scaffold Thins

Osteoporosis reduces bone mass and structural strength, which increases the risk of broken bones. It is often silent until a fracture, and common fracture sites are the hip, spine and wrist.

At a glance

What it does
Reduces bone mass and structural strength
Result
Increased risk of broken bones
Common fracture sites
Hip, spine and wrist
Before a fracture
Often silent
Bone-density test
DXA, commonly at the hip and spine
Risk factors
Older age, estrogen decline after menopause, family history, long-term glucocorticoid use

How the scaffold thins

Osteoporosis reduces bone mass and structural strength, increasing the risk of broken bones. Bone remodeling removes old bone and forms new bone, and bone loss occurs when removal outpaces replacement.

With aging, the cortical outer shell thins and the inner trabecular architecture becomes thinner and less connected. The comparative cutaways in the infographic are illustrative schematics, not diagnostic scans.

Sources: [1] [3]

Fractures

Osteoporosis is often silent until a fracture. The hip, spine and wrist are common fracture sites, and a fracture sometimes follows minor trauma. Vertebral compression fractures may shorten the front of a vertebral body, causing back pain, loss of height and a stooped posture. Not every spinal fracture is due to osteoporosis.

New severe back pain, or pain after a minor fall, warrants prompt clinical assessment for a possible fracture, not self-diagnosis.

Sources: [1] [3] [4]

Risk factors and evaluation

Risk factors include older age, the decline in estrogen after menopause, family history and long-term glucocorticoid use. Men can also develop osteoporosis. Evaluation combines fracture history and medical history with bone-density testing. DXA measures bone mineral density, commonly at the hip and spine, and helps assess fracture risk.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Care and medicines

Care may include adequate calcium, vitamin D and protein, individually appropriate weight-bearing and resistance exercise, balance work and fall prevention at home. Exercise is tailored to fracture risk. Clinician-selected medicines can slow bone loss or build bone and reduce fracture risk. Treatment is individualized, and nutrition alone is not a substitute for medication when it is indicated.

Sources: [2] [3]

Plantar Fasciitis — Load at the Heel

Plantar fasciitis is load-related heel pain involving the plantar fascia, the strong band under the foot that supports the arch. Excess loading can irritate and damage the band, though the cause is not always clear.

At a glance

Tissue involved
Plantar fascia, a strong band on the underside of the foot
What the fascia does
Connects the heel to the front of the foot and supports the arch
Typical pain
Under the heel or arch, worse on first steps after rest
Imaging
May be used to exclude other causes; not routinely needed
Heel spurs
Not the cause of plantar fasciitis pain

The band under the foot

The plantar fascia is a strong band on the underside of the foot. It connects the heel to the front of the foot and supports the arch. Excess loading can irritate and damage it, causing pain under the heel. The cause is not always clear.

Increased activity, long standing on hard surfaces, tight calves and poor shoe support can increase the risk. Heel spurs are not the cause of plantar fasciitis pain. Many people with heel spurs have no pain.

Sources: [1] [2]

How the pain behaves

Pain typically occurs under the heel or arch. It is worse on the first steps after rest and may ease with initial movement. It can worsen with prolonged standing or walking.

Sources: [1] [2]

Assessment and first care

A clinician assesses the symptoms and examines the foot. Imaging may be used to exclude other causes but is not routinely needed.

Initial care includes reducing the activity that aggravates the pain, cushioned supportive shoes or inserts, and gentle stretching of the calf and plantar fascia. A physiotherapist can guide the exercises.

Sources: [1] [2]

When heel pain needs assessment

Worsening or persistent pain, tingling or loss of feeling, and foot pain in someone with diabetes are reasons to seek clinical assessment. Severe heel pain after an injury, a snap or pop during an injury, or being unable to walk warrants urgent assessment. Those signs may indicate a different injury, not plantar fasciitis.

The infographic is general medical education and does not diagnose the cause of heel pain. The guidance behind it is against self-diagnosing heel pain.

Sources: [2] [3]

Psoriasis — Skin Turnover and Inflammation

Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated skin condition. Immune overactivity makes skin cells multiply too quickly, which produces scaly, inflamed patches. It is not contagious.

At a glance

Type of condition
Chronic, immune-mediated
Contagious
No
Common sites
Elbows, knees and scalp, although other sites may be affected
Course
Symptoms can flare, then improve or remit
Flare triggers
Stress and skin injuries can trigger flares

Why the skin builds up

Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated condition. Immune overactivity causes skin cells to multiply too quickly, producing scaly, inflamed patches. Psoriasis is not contagious. Genetics and environmental factors both contribute.

The infographic uses a conceptual cutaway of the skin. It contrasts ordinary skin with the increased cell production and thick, scaly surface of psoriasis. The cutaway is a schematic, not a diagnostic specimen.

Sources: [1] [2]

What the plaques look like

The plaques are dry, itchy, sore and flaky. They commonly affect the elbows, knees and scalp, although other sites may be affected. On white skin, plaques may look pink or red with light scales. On dark brown skin, they may look gray, white, raised and scaly. Symptoms can flare and then improve or remit. Stress and skin injuries can trigger flares.

Sources: [1] [2]

How it is treated

Treatment is individualized by the type of psoriasis, its severity and its location. Moisturizers and prescribed topical treatments can help. More severe disease may need medically supervised light therapy or systemic medicines.

Sources: [1] [2]

When care is needed

Suspected psoriasis, treatment that is not working and side effects are all reasons to see a clinician. Persistent, recurrent joint pain, stiffness and swelling warrant assessment for possible psoriatic arthritis.

Rapidly reddening skin with merging pus-filled bumps calls for emergency care. Fever, shivering or a fast heartbeat may accompany a serious condition or infection. Redness can be harder to see on darker skin.

Sources: [1] [2]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Ear Positions — Read the Whole Cat

A cat's ear position is one cue among several. It is read together with the eyes, whiskers, posture, tail and context, and it is not a guaranteed emotion or a diagnosis.

At a glance

Main rule
Read ears with eyes, whiskers, posture, tail and context
Upright ears
With half-closed eyes, can accompany a relaxed expression
Forward ears
With open eyes, can indicate attention or anxiety
Flattened ears
With whiskers drawn against the face, can accompany fear
Ears back and flat
With whiskers forward, can accompany defensive or aggressive communication

Ears as one cue among several

Ear position is interpreted together with the eyes, whiskers, posture, tail and context. These are contextual cues. They are not a guaranteed emotion or a diagnosis.

Sources: [1] [2]

Upright and forward ears

Upright ears with half-closed eyes can accompany a relaxed expression. Forward ears with open eyes can indicate attention or anxiety. They do not reliably mean happiness.

Sources: [2]

Flattened and backward ears

Flattened ears with whiskers drawn against the face can accompany fear. Fear can also involve a low crouch and a tail that is tucked or wrapped closely. Ears held back and flat with whiskers directed forward can accompany defensive or aggressive communication.

Ears moving backward together with a lashing tail can come before petting-induced aggression. Cornell's veterinary guidance for that moment is to stop petting and allow a cooling-down period without physical contact, and to avoid punishment, restraint or uninvited handling.

Feline Tongue — Backward-Facing Papillae

A cat's tongue bears backward-facing keratin spines called filiform papillae. During grooming, the large ones wick saliva into a cavity at the tip and release it onto the hairs of the coat.

At a glance

Structures
Filiform papillae, backward-facing keratin spines
Direction
Pointing toward the throat
Tip of large papillae
A scoop-shaped, U-shaped cavity
How saliva is held
Wicked into the cavity by surface tension
Behavior

Spines that point toward the throat

Licking is a normal grooming behavior in cats. The tongue bears backward-facing spines of keratin called filiform papillae. They point toward the throat, not toward the tip of the tongue.

Sources: [1] [2]

A cavity that wicks saliva

The large grooming papillae have a scoop-shaped, U-shaped cavity at the tip. The cavity wicks saliva by surface tension. A papilla is not a hollow syringe connected to a salivary duct.

Sources: [1]

The grooming stroke

As the tongue expands, the grooming papillae rotate to stand more erect, which increases their contact with the fur. The tongue presses and compresses the fur during the stroke.

Saliva that was wicked into the papilla cavities is released onto the hairs by contact. The papillae deliver saliva deeper into the coat than the surface of the tongue does alone.

Sources: [1]

Head Bunting — Contact and Scent

Head bunting is a cat approaching and rubbing its head on a person or on another cat. Rubbing the face deposits chemical signals from scent glands, and what the gesture means socially is an interpretation, not a certainty.

At a glance

Behavior
A cat approaching and rubbing its head on a person
Scent glands

What bunting is

Bunting is a cat approaching and rubbing its head on a person. Cats can also bunt one another. Allorubbing, when two cats rub their bodies against each other, is related to a head bunt but distinct from it.

Sources: [1] [2]

Scent left by the face

Cats have scent glands around their cheeks, lips and forehead, and rubbing the face deposits chemical signals. Pheromones are chemical signals used in communication between members of the same species.

Cats rub their faces on familiar objects, including doorways. Facial scent marking occurs in places where cats are comfortable.

Sources: [1]

How bunting is interpreted

Bunting toward people is interpreted as social affiliation and scent marking. It is not proof of a specific thought, and it does not carry one universal emotional meaning.

A cat's thoughts cannot be known directly. Its engagement, its seeking of company and its other behavior give the context for interpreting contentment.

Sources: [1] [2]

Cat Atlas / Household hazards · October 23, 2026

Lily Exposure — Pollen, Petals and Vase Water

True lilies and daylilies can cause potentially fatal kidney failure in cats. A cat can be poisoned by chewing the plant, licking pollen from its fur or drinking the vase water, and small exposures can cause severe harm.

At a glance

Plants involved
True lilies (Lilium species) and daylilies (Hemerocallis species)
Harm to cats
Potentially fatal kidney failure
Hazardous parts
All parts, including stems, leaves, flowers and pollen, plus vase water
Routes of exposure
Chewing plant material, licking pollen from fur, drinking vase water
Toxic substance
Not identified
Early signs
May include vomiting, drooling, loss of appetite and reduced activity

Which lilies are involved

True lilies, which are Lilium species, and daylilies, which are Hemerocallis species, can cause potentially fatal kidney failure in cats. The Easter lily (Lilium longiflorum) is a dangerous true lily. Daylilies belong to Hemerocallis, a distinct genus.

Not every plant called a lily has the same toxin or risk. Peace lilies and calla lilies cause irritation from calcium oxalate, not the kidney toxicity of true lilies. They are still not safe to chew.

Sources: [1] [2]

How cats are exposed

All parts of these plants are hazardous, including the stems, leaves, flowers and pollen. The water in a vase of lilies is hazardous too. Cats can be poisoned by chewing plant material, by licking pollen from their fur while grooming, or by drinking the vase water. Small exposures can cause severe harm. The specific substance that is toxic to the kidneys has not been identified.

Sources: [1]

Signs and what the sources advise

Early signs may include vomiting, drooling, loss of appetite and reduced activity. The guidance from the FDA and Cornell is not to wait for signs before seeking help. Suspected ingestion of lily material, pollen or vase water warrants immediate contact with a veterinarian or pet poison control, and early veterinary treatment improves the outlook.

The same sources advise keeping these lilies out of households with cats, and bringing a photograph or sample of the plant to help with identification when seeking veterinary care. Cornell's guidance is not to induce vomiting unless a veterinarian or poison control professional specifically directs it.

Sources: [1] [2]

The Tapetum — A Second Pass for Light

The tapetum lucidum lies behind the cat's retina and reflects light that the retina did not absorb. The light gets a second pass through the retina, which improves sensitivity in dim light.

At a glance

Structure
Tapetum lucidum
Position
Behind the retina, part of the choroidal tissues
What it does
Reflects unabsorbed light back for a second chance at absorption
Effect
Improved sensitivity in dim light
Light production
None. It reflects incoming light
Microstructure
Ordered groups of slender rodlets in the tapetal cells

The path of light into the eye

The cornea admits light. The iris regulates its entry through the pupil, and the lens focuses the incoming light onto the retina. The optic nerve carries visual information toward the brain.

Sources: [1]

A second pass through the retina

The tapetum lucidum lies behind the retina. It reflects light that was not absorbed on its first passage, giving the retina a second opportunity to absorb it. This improves sensitivity in dim light.

The tapetum is a reflector of incoming light. It is not an organ that produces light. The arrows in the diagram stand for incoming and reflected light, not light that is generated.

Sources: [1] [2]

What the reflector is made of

The tapetal layer is part of the choroidal tissues behind the retina. Tapetal cells in the cat contain ordered groups of slender rodlets. Multilayer reflecting domains account for the reflection, and the wavelength reflected depends on the spacing of the layers in a domain.

The microscopic views in the infographic are schematic and not to scale. The layers may be simplified and exaggerated for explanation. They are not a full clinical histology section.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Water in the Bowl and the Food

Cats take in water by drinking and through the moisture in their food. Because food contributes water, the bowl alone does not measure how much a cat takes in.

At a glance

Sources of water

Water from food and from the bowl

Cats take in water both by drinking and through moisture in their food. Wet food can contain up to 80% water. Cats eating wet food may drink less, while cats fed dry food generally get more of their water by drinking.

Cornell's feeding guidance gives typical figures by food format: dry cat food contains 6 to 10% water, and canned food contains at least 75% water. These are typical values for each kind of food, not feeding ratios. Because food contributes water, the bowl alone does not measure a cat's total water intake.

Sources: [1] [2]

Fresh water and wet food

The veterinary sources say that cats should always have access to clean, fresh water, even when they eat wet food. Wet food can help increase water intake, but a diet should still be complete and balanced.

This is general education, not an intake prescription for an individual cat. If dehydration is suspected, the guidance is to contact a veterinarian promptly.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Phobias · October 24, 2026

Chiroptophobia — Fear of Bats

Chiroptophobia means fear of bats. It is a descriptive name, not a separately named diagnosis, and a phobia is different from ordinary caution around wildlife.

At a glance

Meaning
Fear of bats
Status
A descriptive fear name; clinically significant animal fears can fall under specific phobia
Possible body signs
Palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness; symptoms differ between people
Treatment
CBT, with exposure therapy a particularly effective method for phobias
Bat safety
Bats usually avoid humans; the guidance is not to touch them

The name and its status

Chiroptophobia means fear of bats. Monash University uses that spelling. The word is used here as a descriptive fear name. Clinically significant fears of animals can fall under specific phobia, not under a separately named bat diagnosis.

A phobia involves fear out of proportion to actual danger. It is not simply ordinary caution around wildlife.

Sources: [1] [2] [4]

Encounters, anticipation and avoidance

The infographic is general education, not diagnosis. The sources advise consulting a healthcare professional when fear affects daily life.

Masklophobia — Fear of Masks and Costumed Characters

Masklophobia is a descriptive term from cognitive-science research for fear of costumed characters, with fear of masks a related documented presentation. It is not a standalone diagnosis, and the research on what contributes to it is preliminary.

At a glance

A descriptive name

Masklophobia is a descriptive term used in cognitive-science research for fear of costumed characters. Fear of masks is a related, documented presentation. The definition the infographic displays is fear of masks and costumed characters.

In the cited research, masklophobia is not listed as a separately named DSM-5 disorder. A descriptive name is not a standalone diagnosis, and educational information does not diagnose an individual.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

What the research examined

Masks and costumed characters can be fear triggers. The research examined imagined encounters with masked people, with occupied costumes and with unoccupied costumes. Responses vary.

Preliminary questionnaire research suggests that face concealment and movement may contribute to fear of costumed characters. These are possible contributors, not a proven universal cause.

A person can know that a costume is not actually dangerous and still feel fear. The feeling of alarm does not establish that the object is a threat.

Sources: [1] [2]

Symptoms and avoidance

Phobia symptoms can include severe anxiety and worry, palpitations, trembling, chest tightness and nausea. The infographic shows a racing heart, trembling and worry as possible symptoms, not universal ones.

Phobic fear can lead to avoidance, including avoiding places where feared objects may be encountered, and avoidance can restrict daily life. The infographic traces a path from cue to anxiety to avoidance to restricted activities. That path is not a claimed brain circuit.

Sources: [2] [3]

Treatment evidence comes from phobias generally

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a treatment for phobias. Gradual exposure supported by a therapist is a general phobia treatment. It is not the result of a trial in masklophobia, and it is not a prescription for self-directed exposure. Professional help is relevant when phobia symptoms affect everyday life.

Sources: [2] [3]

Specific Phobia — Horses

An intense fear of horses that disrupts daily life falls under the clinical category of specific phobia. Perceived danger can exceed actual danger, yet horses are powerful animals and ordinary handling precautions remain important.

At a glance

Clinical category
Specific phobia, not a separate horse-specific diagnosis
Definition shown
Intense fear of horses that disrupts daily life
Possible triggers
Encountering or thinking about a horse
Possible body signs
Fast heartbeat, shaking, tense muscles; symptoms vary
Real safety
Horses are powerful and can kick
Approach that can help
CBT; graded exposure in small manageable steps

The clinical category

Specific phobia is the clinical category used here. It is not a separately invented horse-specific diagnosis. The definition the infographic displays for this subject is an intense fear of horses that disrupts daily life. Its scene, an adult beside a sunlit paddock, is fictional.

Sources: [1] [2]

Triggers, worry and fight-or-flight

Phobic fear can be triggered by encountering the feared animal or by thinking about it. In the fictional illustration, a horse and an imagined horse represent those triggers. Anticipatory anxiety means worry before an encounter. Thoughts about the feared animal can trigger anxiety and physical symptoms.

Fight-or-flight arousal is the body preparing for perceived danger. A fast heartbeat, shaking and tense muscles can occur, but symptoms vary.

Avoidance can quickly reduce anxiety. It can also maintain fear, because it prevents learning about the feared situation and about the ability to cope.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Fear and real horse safety

Perceived danger can exceed actual danger, and ordinary animal-handling precautions remain important. Horses are powerful and can kick, so treatment for fear must not be confused with ignoring real safety. Realistic horse safety includes respecting distance and obtaining knowledgeable supervision, not attempting to handle a horse unsupervised.

Sources: [1] [2] [4]

Graded steps, not forced confrontation

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can help with phobias. Graded exposure involves small, manageable steps, not forced confrontation. Seeking a qualified clinician is appropriate when symptoms affect life.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Specific Phobia — Mice and Rats

An intense, disproportionate fear of mice and rats falls under the clinical category of specific phobia. It is distinct from ordinary caution around animals, which still has a place: mice and rats can carry germs, and small mammals can bite.

At a glance

Clinical category
Specific phobia, for an animal-related fear

Intense, disproportionate fear of mice and rats

Phobia and ordinary caution

This fear is described with the clinical category of specific phobia, applied to an animal-related fear. It is not a separate invented diagnosis. Specific phobia involves fear out of proportion to actual danger. Ordinary caution around animals is distinct from disabling phobic fear.

Sources: [1] [2]

Triggers and body alarm

Encountering the feared animal, or anticipating an encounter, may provoke intense fear, anxiety and active avoidance. The encounter in a shed shown on the infographic is a fictional example, not a clinical case or a universal trigger.

Anticipatory anxiety means worry before an encounter. Even thinking about feared situations can cause anxiety and avoidance. Autonomic arousal is the body alarm associated with fear. A noticeable heartbeat and trembling can occur, but symptoms vary.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

How relief can reinforce avoidance

Negative reinforcement can maintain avoidance. The short-term relief that follows avoiding a feared situation can make avoidance more likely again. This is a possible learning mechanism, not an explanation of every case.

Sources: [3]

Germs, bites and ordinary caution

Mice and rats can carry germs, and small mammals can bite. Guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is to be cautious with unfamiliar animals and to wash hands after handling small mammals or their supplies. Therapy does not mean ignoring genuine animal-related hazards.

Sources: [4]

Treatment planned with a clinician

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an evidence-based treatment, and exposure therapy is a particularly effective CBT method for phobias. A clinician and patient can plan work on avoided situations. Treatment can help and is individualized. Professional help is relevant when fear affects daily life.

The help shown on the infographic is a collaborative conversation about a photograph of an animal. It is not a set of instructions to approach or handle wild rodents.

Trypophobia — Clusters of Holes

Trypophobia is a name used in scientific research for fear of, or aversion to, images of clusters of holes. Research describes a visual pattern in triggering images, but not a proven universal cause.

At a glance

Meaning
Fear or aversion to images of clusters of holes
Name used in
Scientific research
Example triggers
Lotus seed pod, soap bubbles, aerated chocolate; responses vary between people
Reported reactions
Some people report sweating, panic and increased heart rate
Research finding
Relatively high contrast energy at midrange spatial frequencies in triggering images

General to phobias; a trypophobia-specific benefit is not established by these sources

The name and its triggers

Trypophobia is a name used in scientific research for fear of, or aversion to, images of clusters of holes. A lotus seed pod, soap bubbles and aerated chocolate are examples of visual triggers. Responses vary between people. Some people report sweating, panic and an increased heart rate when viewing clustered holes.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

What research found in the images

Research found relatively high contrast energy at midrange spatial frequencies in triggering images. That finding describes the structure of the visual pattern. It is not a proven universal cause, and it is not a diagnostic test.

Sources: [1] [2]

Alarm, relief and avoidance

Fear can activate a heightened fight-or-flight response even in situations that are not really dangerous. An alarm response does not establish that an ordinary seed pod in a picture is dangerous.

Avoiding feared situations can bring short-term relief while maintaining or increasing fear over time. Negative reinforcement is the technical label for this loop, in which relief keeps avoidance going.

Sources: [4]

Support, and the limits of the evidence

For phobias in general, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and gradual exposure can help. These sources do not establish a treatment benefit specific to trypophobia. A clinician can assess symptoms and their impact on life and plan appropriate support.

The sources advise seeking help when symptoms affect daily life. Triggering images online may be distressing, and people should not be pushed into viewing them.

Sources: [3] [4]

Dactylotum bicolor — The Painted Grasshopper

Dactylotum bicolor, the pictured or painted grasshopper, is a flightless grasshopper of the western Great Plains. Its red and yellow warning colors signal to potential predators that it is unpalatable.

At a glance

Scientific name
Dactylotum bicolor
Common names
Pictured grasshopper, painted grasshopper
Range
Western Great Plains, from Alberta to northern Mexico
Habitat
Shortgrass prairie and sparse low vegetation
Food
Forbs (herbaceous flowering plants), not grasses
Adult length
About 25 mm for males and 32 mm for females

Warning colors

The grasshopper's red and yellow warning coloration signals unpalatability to potential predators. This kind of signal is called aposematism. It does not establish that the grasshopper carries a toxin, or that every predator avoids it.

The adult described for Colorado has black and yellow bands, a red-orange midline, red-orange markings on the face and thorax, black and red-orange hind femora and yellow-green hind tibiae. Coloration varies geographically.

Sources: [1] [2]

Body and reduced wings

Adults have a vertical face, a rounded top to the head, slender antennae and a cylindrical, pitted pronotum crossed by three incisions. The tegmina (forewings) and the wings are very small, and this grasshopper is flightless. The small black tegmina have fine yellow veins. In the University of Wyoming account, adult length is about 25 mm for males and 32 mm for females.

Sources: [1] [2]

Where it lives and what it eats

The painted grasshopper occurs in shortgrass prairie and sparse low vegetation along the western Great Plains, from Alberta to northern Mexico. It feeds on forbs, which are herbaceous flowering plants, and not on grasses. Reported food plants include scarlet globemallow and prairie clover.

Sources: [1] [2]

One generation a year

The species produces one generation a year. Females lay eggs in soft soil or sand in fall. The eggs overwinter underground and hatch in late spring to early summer. The eggs are brownish-yellow and lie in underground pods, laid in disorderly columns.

Sources: [1] [2]

The generalized digestive diagram

The internal view in the infographic is a simplified, generalized insect digestive plan, not a dissection of Dactylotum. It shows an alimentary canal running from mouth to anus, with a foregut, midgut and hindgut. In the generalized insect gut, the crop stores food, the midgut is the main site of enzymatic digestion and nutrient absorption, and the hindgut regulates the recovery of water and salt from waste.

Sources: [3]

Enceladus — Ocean Escaping Through Ice

Enceladus is an icy moon of Saturn, about 500 kilometers across, with a global salty ocean beneath its crust. Jets near its south pole release water vapor and ice grains from that ocean.

An ocean under ice

Enceladus is an icy moon of Saturn, about 500 kilometers across. A global ocean of salty liquid water lies beneath its icy crust, above a rocky core.

Sources: [1] [2]

Jets from the tiger stripes

Fractures near the south pole, informally called tiger stripes, release jets of water vapor and ice grains from the subsurface ocean. Some of the ejected material falls back to the surface. Some escapes and supplies Saturn's E ring.

Cassini sampled the plume and detected water, salts, organic materials and silica particles. These are chemical clues, not evidence that life has been found. No life has been confirmed on Enceladus, and being potentially habitable is not the same as a detection of organisms.

Sources: [1] [2]

What may heat the interior

The silica particles support the idea that hot water interacts with rock in the interior. Hydrothermal circulation is inferred, not photographed. Saturn's tides deform Enceladus as it follows an elliptical orbit, and tidal friction is a proposed source of internal heat.

In one proposed model the core is porous. Ocean water enters the deformable rock, is heated by tidal friction and rises back toward the ocean. The detailed interior and the distribution of heat remain modeled, not directly observed.

The cutaway and the orbit in the infographic are schematic. Layer thicknesses, the eccentricity of the orbit, jet size and particle size are not to scale.

Gyrinus substriatus — Eyes Above and Below

Gyrinus substriatus is a black whirligig beetle of pools and ponds, common and widespread in Britain. Whirligig beetles have divided eyes that see above and below the water at the same time.

Identifying the species

Gyrinus substriatus is a whirligig beetle with a black body and yellow legs. Adults are 5 to 7.5 mm long. The pronotum has a lip along its side and an inner groove. The claws on the middle and hind feet are not darkened, and the rim of the wing covers is approximately parallel along its length. The species occurs in pools and ponds, and it is common and widespread in Britain.

Sources: [2]

Eyes above and below the water

The eyes of whirligig beetles are divided. The upper parts see above the water while the lower parts see below it, at the same time. Whirligig beetles also have short, thick antennae, long grasping forelegs, and short, flattened, paddle-like middle and hind legs.

They whirl at the surface, often in groups, seeking dead or injured insects, and they dive when disturbed. The divided eyes and paddle legs are described for the whirligig family as a whole.

Sources: [1]

Larvae and pupae

Whirligig larvae are aquatic predators of aquatic invertebrates. They have gills on the abdomen, and they leave the water to pupate in a cocoon above the waterline. In Gyrinus substriatus, both the larvae and the adults are predatory, and the species pupates on land in a cocoon of plant matter and sand grains.

Sources: [1] [2]

The generalized digestive diagram

The internal digestive view in the infographic is a generalized insect schematic, not a dissection of this species. Food passes from the mouth to the foregut, the midgut, the hindgut and the anus. In this general plan, the midgut is a principal site of digestion and nutrient absorption, and the hindgut recovers water and salts.

Sources: [3]

Magicicada septendecim — Seventeen Years to Sing

Magicicada septendecim, Linnaeus' 17-year cicada, normally spends 17 years as a nymph underground, feeding on root fluids. Adult males then sing with paired, muscle-driven membranes called tymbals.

At a glance

Scientific name
Magicicada septendecim
Common name
Linnaeus' 17-year cicada
Family
Cicadidae
Adult length
About one and one-half inches
Life cycle
Normally 17 years, with occasional early or late stragglers
Where
Eastern North America; 17-year species are generally northern

How to recognize it

Magicicada septendecim is a true bug in the family Cicadidae. Adults have black bodies, red to reddish-orange eyes, six legs, and transparent wings with orange veins. This species has broad orange bands on the underside of the abdomen and orange on the thorax behind each eye.

Adult periodical cicadas are about one and one-half inches long. The infographic's small, approximately life-size silhouette and 1 cm ruler give an approximate scale. They are not the measurements of a specimen.

Sources: [1] [3] [4]

How the male sings

Male periodical cicadas produce airborne songs with paired ridged membranes called tymbals, on the first segment of the abdomen. Large muscles drive the tymbals, and the vibrating membrane produces airborne sound. The male abdomen is hollow and may act as a resonating chamber.

The infographic's internal view of the sound organs is a simplified schematic of a male periodical cicada, not a measured dissection of this species. Its arrows show cause. They do not show a measured frequency or amount of movement.

Sources: [2] [3]

Hearing and choruses

Both sexes hear with membranous tympana on the underside of the abdomen. Tympana are hearing organs and are distinct from the sound-producing tymbals. The calling songs of males attract both males and females to choruses, often in high, sunlit branches. Female Magicicada respond to male calls with timed wing flicks.

Sources: [2]

Seventeen years underground

Nymphs live underground and feed on root fluids. Magicicada septendecim normally has a 17-year life cycle, with occasional stragglers that appear early or late. Mature nymphs emerge, climb vegetation and molt into pale adults that later darken. There is no pupal stage.

Females insert their eggs into living twigs with an ovipositor. The hatchlings drop and burrow into the soil to begin feeding on roots.

Sources: [1] [3] [4]

Range, food and predators

Periodical cicadas occur in eastern North America. The 17-year species are generally northern, and they overlap with the southern 13-year species. Adults use living deciduous woody vegetation.

Periodical cicadas feed on plant fluids and are eaten by birds and other animals. A mass emergence can satiate predators, but it does not guarantee the survival of each cicada.

Sources: [3] [4]

Pulsar — The Sweeping Lighthouse

A pulsar is a rapidly rotating, magnetized neutron star. Its beams sweep through space as it rotates, and when one crosses Earth the star appears to switch on and off like a lighthouse.

A rapidly rotating magnetized neutron star

A rotating magnetized remnant

A pulsar is a rapidly rotating, magnetized neutron star. A neutron star is the remnant core of a massive star after an explosion. Strong magnetic fields, and the electric fields associated with them, accelerate particles, and those particles emit radiation. The emission of a pulsar includes radio waves.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Why the beams sweep

The beams emerge in the directions of the magnetic poles. The magnetic axis can be offset from the rotation axis, and that offset causes the beams to sweep through space as the star rotates.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

What an observer sees

A beam that crosses Earth makes the pulsar appear to switch on and off like a lighthouse. The regular pulses that are observed reflect the rotation of the star. A schematic signal has a peak when a beam crosses the line of sight and a low interval when the beam points away. Geometry controls whether an observer sees pulses.

The curved field lines and opposing beams in the infographic are schematic representations of the magnetic geometry. They are not visible solid structures.

Radiocarbon — The Isotope Clock

Radiocarbon, or carbon-14, forms in the upper atmosphere and enters living things through carbon dioxide and food. After a sample stops exchanging carbon, its carbon-14 decays, and the amount that remains is used to infer an age.

At a glance

Carbon-12
Six protons and six neutrons; stable
Carbon-14
Six protons and eight neutrons; radioactive
Where carbon-14 forms
In the upper atmosphere, from nitrogen-14
Decays to
Nitrogen
What is measured
Remaining radiocarbon relative to stable carbon
Applies to
Once-living material that contains carbon

How carbon-14 forms and enters life

Carbon-12 has six protons and six neutrons and is stable. Carbon-14 has six protons and eight neutrons and is radioactive. Cascades of cosmic rays produce neutrons in the upper atmosphere. Nitrogen-14 captures a neutron and emits a proton, forming carbon-14.

Radiocarbon in the atmosphere enters carbon dioxide. Plants take up carbon dioxide by photosynthesis, and animals acquire carbon through their food.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

The decay clock

After a sample stops exchanging carbon with its surroundings, the ratio of radiocarbon to stable carbon decreases exponentially through radioactive decay. Carbon-14 decays to nitrogen. An ideal closed sample retains half of its initial carbon-14 after each half-life, so the relative sequence runs 100%, 50%, 25%, 12.5%. The decay curve approaches zero. It does not drop in a straight line.

Radiocarbon dating uses that decline. It measures the radiocarbon that remains in a sample, relative to stable carbon, to infer an age.

Sources: [2] [3]

Limits on what a date means

The method applies to carbon-containing material that was once living. Stone and metal usually cannot be dated directly by radiocarbon. A date from wood records the growth of the tree ring that was sampled, not necessarily when the wood was used.

Radiocarbon in the atmosphere has varied, so calendar ages need calibration against material of known age. Contamination can introduce carbon of another age, and chemical pretreatment aims to remove it. Marine reservoir effects can shift apparent ages, because carbon in the ocean differs from carbon in the atmosphere.

Sources: [2] [3]

Bell’s Palsy — The Interrupted Facial Signal

Bell's palsy usually causes weakness or paralysis on one side of the face. It comes on suddenly and its exact cause is unknown. Sudden facial droop can also indicate a stroke, which warrants an immediate emergency call.

At a glance

The facial nerve

The facial nerve, cranial nerve VII, connects the brain to the muscles that control facial expression. It also affects taste and sensation in the ear. Bell's palsy usually causes weakness or paralysis on one side of the face. The exact cause is unknown. Inflammation and swelling of the facial nerve may be involved.

Sources: [1] [2]

How it appears

Symptoms develop suddenly, over hours to a few days, and may involve both the upper and lower muscles of the face. They can include a drooping eyebrow or mouth, difficulty closing the eyelid, a dry or watering eye, drooling and altered taste.

Sources: [1] [2]

Stroke warning signs

Sudden facial droop, arm weakness or speech difficulty can indicate a stroke and warrant an immediate emergency call. Bell's palsy is not a condition to self-diagnose.

Sources: [2]

Assessment, treatment and recovery

Clinicians assess facial movement and how the symptoms began, and they rule out other causes. No single laboratory test confirms Bell's palsy. Prompt medical assessment matters because prescribed steroids are most effective when started within 72 hours, where they are suitable. Antivirals are sometimes added.

If the eyelid cannot close, lubricating drops or ointment and eyelid protection at night, used under a clinician's guidance, help prevent drying and injury to the eye. Many people recover within weeks to six months, but recovery may take longer and some weakness can persist.

Sources: [1] [2]
