COPD — Air That Cannot Easily Leave

COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, is damage to the lungs and airways that restricts airflow and makes breathing difficult. It has no cure, but treatments can improve symptoms and the ability to stay active.

At a glance

Full name
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Disease patterns
Chronic bronchitis and emphysema, in a varying mixture for most people
Confirming test
Spirometry, a breathing test
Contributing exposures
Long-term tobacco smoke, air pollution, occupational dust or fumes
Cure
None; treatments can improve symptoms

How airflow is limited

Airways carry air to elastic air sacs called alveoli. Normal air sacs fill on inhalation and deflate on exhalation. In COPD, damage to the lungs and airways restricts airflow and makes breathing difficult.

Chronic bronchitis involves an inflamed, swollen airway lining and excess mucus that narrow or clog the airways. Emphysema damages the walls between alveoli and reduces elasticity, which makes it harder to move air out. Most people with COPD have a varying mixture of emphysema and chronic bronchitis.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Symptoms, exposures and testing

Symptoms include breathlessness, especially with activity, a chronic cough with or without mucus, wheezing and fatigue. Long-term tobacco smoke, air pollution and occupational dust or fumes can contribute to COPD. Not everyone with COPD has smoked. Spirometry is a breathing test used to confirm COPD. Symptoms alone are not a diagnosis.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

What care involves

COPD has no cure, but treatments can improve symptoms and the ability to stay active. Quitting smoking, avoiding lung irritants, appropriate vaccinations and pulmonary rehabilitation are parts of COPD care.

Bronchodilator inhalers relax the airway muscles and help keep the airways open. Correct inhaler technique matters, and care is individualized. Oxygen therapy is used when it is indicated for low blood oxygen, not routinely for everyone with COPD.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Flare-ups and emergencies

A sudden worsening is called a flare-up, or exacerbation. Suddenly worse symptoms are a reason to contact a healthcare provider right away. Severe trouble catching a breath or talking calls for emergency care.

Sources: [2] [3] [4]

Endometriosis — Tissue Outside Its Usual Home

Endometriosis is a chronic disease in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus, causing inflammation and scar tissue. Its cause is unknown, and symptoms vary from person to person.

At a glance

What it is
Tissue similar to the uterine lining growing outside the uterus
Common lesion sites
Ovaries, fallopian tubes, behind the uterus, and bowel or bladder surfaces
Cause
Unknown
Prevention
No known method
Cure
None known; symptoms or lesions can recur after treatment

Where the tissue grows

The endometrium is the lining of the uterus. In endometriosis, tissue similar to that lining grows outside the uterus, causing inflammation and scar tissue. It is a chronic disease. The infographic sets it in the anatomy of the pelvis: the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, bladder and bowel. Lesions commonly occur on the ovaries and fallopian tubes, behind the uterus, and on the surfaces of the bowel or bladder. The cause is unknown, and no known method prevents endometriosis.

Sources: [1] [2]

Symptoms that vary

Symptoms vary. They include severe period pain, persistent pelvic pain, painful sex, painful bowel movements or urination, and difficulty conceiving. Some people have no symptoms. The size and location of lesions do not reliably correspond to how severe the pain is or where it is felt.

Sources: [1] [2]

Evaluation and treatment

Clinical history and imaging such as ultrasound or MRI help with evaluation. Laparoscopy may confirm a diagnosis but is not always required before treatment.

Treatment is individualized to symptoms, preferences and pregnancy goals. Pain medicines, hormonal treatment, selected surgery and fertility care may help. Hormonal methods may not suit people who are trying to conceive. There is no known cure, and symptoms or lesions can recur after treatment. Multidisciplinary pain care, including physiotherapy and emotional support, can help.

Sources: [1]

Pelvic pain warning signs

Pelvic pain has other possible causes, and it is not something to self-diagnose as endometriosis. Severe or worsening pelvic pain, fainting or heavy vaginal bleeding calls for emergency care. Pelvic pain with fever or a possible pregnancy calls for urgent assessment. These are general warnings about pelvic pain.

Sources: [3]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Macular Degeneration — The Center of Sight

Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) damages the macula, the part of the retina that supports sharp, straight-ahead central vision. Its exact cause is unknown, and treatment depends on the type and stage.

At a glance

Part affected
The macula, part of the retina at the back of the eye
Vision affected
Sharp, straight-ahead central vision
Risk factors
Age, family history and smoking
Disease patterns
Dry AMD and wet AMD
Evaluation
Comprehensive dilated eye examination and OCT imaging
Wet AMD treatment
Anti-VEGF eye injections

The macula and central vision

The macula is part of the light-sensitive retina at the back of the eye. It supports sharp, straight-ahead central vision. AMD damages the macula with aging. Its exact cause is unknown. Age, family history and smoking increase the risk.

Sources: [1] [2]

Dry and wet AMD

Dry AMD can feature yellow drusen beneath the retina and can progress to retinal atrophy. Wet AMD features abnormal vessels beneath the retina that may leak or bleed and distort the structure of the retina. These are different disease patterns, not a single sequence that every case follows.

Sources: [2]

Changes in vision

Early AMD may have no symptoms. Advanced disease can make straight lines look wavy and can blur or blank out central vision. Peripheral vision is generally preserved, which is different from complete blindness.

New wavy lines or changes in central vision require prompt assessment by an eye doctor. Straight lines that look wavy warrant seeing an eye doctor right away.

Sources: [1] [2]

Evaluation and care

A comprehensive dilated eye examination and OCT imaging can help evaluate AMD. Treatment depends on the type and stage. Anti-VEGF eye injections treat wet AMD and can preserve vision. Selected patients with intermediate AMD may benefit from AREDS-type supplements recommended by a clinician. That is not a recommendation of supplements for everyone.

Quitting smoking, regular exercise and healthy eating may help lower the risk or slow AMD-related vision loss. Low-vision devices and rehabilitation can support daily activities.

Sources: [1] [2]

Rheumatoid Arthritis — An Inflamed Joint Lining

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of joints, causing inflammation, pain, stiffness and swelling. There is no current cure, but early diagnosis and appropriate treatment can ease symptoms and reduce joint damage.

At a glance

Type of condition
Chronic autoimmune disease
Tissue attacked
The lining of joints
Joints commonly affected
Small joints in the hands, wrists and feet
Pattern
Often symmetrical on both sides, but presentations vary
Commonly prescribed
Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs)
Cure
None currently

An attack on the joint lining

RA is a chronic autoimmune disease. The immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of joints, causing inflammation, pain, stiffness and swelling. Over time, joint inflammation can damage cartilage and nearby bone. The infographic's schematic joint shows the lining, cartilage and bone. It does not show damage that is inevitable in every patient.

What triggers the immune attack is not fully understood. Smoking and family history are risk factors, not guarantees of disease.

Sources: [2] [3]

Which joints, and how it feels

Small joints in the hands, wrists and feet are commonly affected. Symptoms often occur symmetrically, on both sides, but presentations vary. Common symptoms include tender, warm, swollen joints, prolonged stiffness after waking or rest, difficulty making a fist and fatigue.

Sources: [1] [2]

Diagnosis and treatment

Early clinical evaluation matters. Diagnosis uses examination, blood tests and imaging, not symptoms alone. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment can ease symptoms and reduce joint damage, though there is no current cure.

Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) are commonly prescribed, and a rheumatologist individualizes treatment and follow-up. Low-impact exercise and physiotherapy or occupational therapy can support strength, mobility and daily activities. Supplements do not replace RA medicines.

Sources: [2] [3]

A sudden, severe joint

Sudden severe joint pain with swelling, difficulty moving the joint or fever needs urgent assessment for a possible joint infection. It is not something to assume is an RA flare, and fever may be absent. General education of this kind is distinct from a professional medical diagnosis and individualized treatment.

Sources: [2] [4]

Permethrin — A Dog Treatment That Can Poison Cats

Concentrated permethrin spot-on flea treatments intended for dogs can cause severe, potentially fatal poisoning in cats. A cat can be exposed when the product is applied to it, or through close contact with a recently treated dog.

At a glance

Product
Concentrated dog-only permethrin spot-on flea treatments
Risk to cats
Severe, potentially fatal poisoning
Routes of exposure
Application to a cat; close contact with, or grooming, a recently treated dog
Body system affected
Nervous system
Signs

A dog treatment that can poison cats

Concentrated permethrin spot-on flea treatments intended for dogs can cause severe, potentially fatal poisoning in cats. The guidance from the PDSA veterinary charity and the UK Veterinary Medicines Directorate is never to apply a dog-only flea treatment to a cat, not even part of a pipette.

Cats can also be exposed through close contact with a dog that was recently treated with permethrin, or by grooming it. The guidance is to keep cats away from treated dogs according to the product instructions.

Sources: [1] [2]

Signs and urgent contact

Permethrin toxicity affects the cat's nervous system. It can cause drooling, wobbling, twitching, tremors and seizures. Suspected exposure warrants immediate contact with a veterinarian, even before signs develop. The guidance is to take the product packaging to the vet.

Sources: [1] [2]

What the warning covers

The warning concerns concentrated spot-on products that are for dogs only. It is not a claim that every flea product, or every permethrin formulation, carries an identical risk. The guidance is to check which species a product is suitable for and to follow the product label.

Sources: [1] [2]

The Moving Pinna — A Sound-Collecting Ear

The pinna is the cat's external ear flap. It can orient independently of the head, and its shape contributes to locating sounds, though the precise contribution of active pinna movements is not fully resolved.

At a glance

Pinna
The external ear flap
Movement

The path of sound

The pinna is the external ear flap. Sound vibrations enter the ear canal and reach the eardrum. Small bones in the middle ear transmit them to the inner ear. The cochlea receives the vibrations and passes nervous-system signals toward the brain, which enables hearing.

Sources: [1]

Ears that move independently of the head

A cat's pinnae can orient independently of the position of its head. Pinna movements accompany orienting to sounds and to visual targets.

In the reported experimental conditions, a sound can evoke an early pinna movement that comes before the eye movement. That movement is asymmetric, larger in the ear on the side of the sound. The ear positions in the artwork are illustrative, not a universal fixed response.

Sources: [2]

How the ear helps locate sound

The pinna, head and torso weaken or strengthen different sound frequencies depending on the direction a sound comes from. This creates direction-dependent spectral cues for locating the sound.

The shape of the pinna contributes to sound localization. The precise functional contribution of active pinna movements is not fully resolved. The infographic does not claim perfect localization or a quantified improvement from moving the ears.

Sources: [2]

The Slow Blink — Eyes in Social Context

A cat's slow blink is typically a run of half-blinks followed by longer eye narrowing or closure. Experiments suggest it may be a positive signal between cats and people, but it is read together with the rest of the face and body, not on its own.

At a glance

What it is
Half-blinks followed by prolonged eye narrowing or eye closure
What moves
The eyelids
What it may mean
Possibly positive cat-human communication, not proof of affection every time
Read it with
Ears, tail, pupils and the rest of the body

What a slow blink looks like

A slow blink sequence typically involves half-blinks followed by prolonged eye narrowing or eye closure. It is a movement of the eyelids, and the infographic shows the eyelids moving, not the pupils changing size.

Sources: [1]

What the experiments found

In controlled experiments, cats half-blinked and narrowed their eyes more after their owners slow blinked than when there was no interaction. Cats were also more likely to approach an unfamiliar experimenter after slow blinking than after a neutral expression.

The results suggest that slow blinking may be a positive form of communication between cats and people. They do not make it a guaranteed translation of what a cat feels, or proof of affection in every instance.

Sources: [1]

Reading the whole cat

One eye signal does not stand alone. The face and the body posture supply the context. A relaxed cat can have upright ears and a tail that is not flicking and has no raised hairs.

Backward or flattened ears, a lashing tail and dilated pupils can come before petting-induced aggression. The veterinary guidance behind this part of the infographic is to stop petting when signs of aggression appear and to avoid handling a cat that has not invited it.

Sources: [1] [2]

Tortoiseshell — A Mosaic of Active X Chromosomes

Tortoiseshell cats have mottled orange and non-orange fur and are nearly always female. The patches arise because one X chromosome is randomly inactivated in each cell early in development.

At a glance

Coat
Mottled orange and non-orange fur
Sex
Nearly always female
Source of the patches
Random inactivation of one X chromosome in each cell
Gene region
X-linked ARHGAP36 locus
Pigments
Orange patches favor pheomelanin; black patches favor eumelanin

How the mosaic forms

Tortoiseshell cats have mottled orange and non-orange fur, and they are nearly always female. In a typical XX cat that carries both orange and non-orange variants, one X chromosome is randomly inactivated in each cell early in development.

The cells descended from those early cells retain different active X chromosomes. The result is a mosaic of pigment-cell areas, which appear as orange or black patches in the coat.

Sources: [1] [2]

The orange variant

University accounts of two 2025 studies describe the deletion associated with orange fur. It is in a non-coding region at the ARHGAP36 locus, which is X-linked. Orange patches show increased ARHGAP36 activity in melanocytes, the pigment cells. Orange patches favor the pigment pheomelanin, and black patches favor eumelanin.

Sources: [1] [2]

What the pattern does not show

The cell and chromosome artwork in the infographic is a simplified schematic of the mechanism, not a literal map of a cat's patches.

A coat-color pattern does not establish an individual cat's personality. These findings do not establish links between coat color and behavior.

Sources: [1] [2]

Chronophobia — Extreme Fear of Time or Time Passing

Chronophobia is an extreme fear of time or of time passing. It is a named fear described clinically within specific phobias, and the name does not imply a separate diagnostic code.

At a glance

Meaning
Extreme fear of time or time passing
Status
Named fear described clinically within specific phobias
What can evoke it
Thinking about time passing, getting older or mortality
Possible symptoms
Palpitations, trembling, dizziness; symptoms vary between people
Help
Psychotherapy; CBT is a treatment for phobias

What the name covers

Chronophobia means an extreme fear of time or time passing. It is a named fear described clinically within specific phobias. The name does not imply a separate diagnostic code.

Thinking about time passing, getting older or mortality can evoke intense discomfort or dread. Some people obsess over clocks or calendar days.

Sources: [1]

Symptoms, avoidance and isolation

Phobia symptoms can include palpitations, trembling and dizziness, and symptoms vary between people. People with specific phobias may avoid reminders of what they fear. Chronophobia can involve social isolation and interference with relationships.

Time cannot be stopped. A calendar or a clock is not itself an immediate danger, even when the alarm associated with it feels intense.

Sources: [1] [2]

Therapy and managing symptoms

Psychotherapy can help with chronophobia, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a treatment for phobias. Talking to someone trusted and relaxation breathing may help manage symptoms. The NHS guidance is to seek professional help when symptoms affect daily life.

Sources: [1] [2]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Megalophobia — Intense Fear of Large Objects

Megalophobia is an established name for an intense fear of large objects. It is discussed clinically as a specific phobia, not as a separately named DSM diagnosis.

The name and the triggers

Megalophobia is an established name for intense fear of large objects. It is discussed clinically as a specific phobia, not as a separately named DSM diagnosis. Large buildings, statues and vehicles can trigger the fear. Thinking about large objects can also provoke anticipatory anxiety.

Sources: [1]

Symptoms and proportion

Symptoms can include a rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, dizziness and an urge to escape. Experiences vary. Phobic fear is out of proportion to the actual danger of the object or situation.

Sources: [1]

Avoidance and daily life

Avoidance can provide short-term relief. It also prevents a person from learning that fear can be managed and that feared outcomes often do not happen. Anxiety symptoms can interfere with daily routines and activities, and professional assessment is relevant when fear limits daily life.

Sources: [1] [2]

How gradual exposure is described

Cognitive behavioral therapy helps change responses to anxiety. Gradual exposure therapy is tailored to the person by a therapist or psychologist. Exposure treatment can begin with talking about large objects, then move to pictures, then to being near an object. The pace is gradual and individualized.

Sources: [1]

Nosophobia — Persistent Fear of Developing a Specific Serious Disease

Nosophobia, also called disease phobia, is a persistent fear of developing a specific serious disease. It overlaps with health anxiety and illness anxiety disorder, and which diagnosis applies is for a clinician to assess, not something a label can settle.

At a glance

Meaning
Persistent fear of developing a specific serious disease
Also called
Disease phobia
Overlapping terms
Health anxiety and illness anxiety disorder
Cues
Bodily sensations and disease-related health information
Behaviors that may follow
Body checking, searching for health information, seeking reassurance, avoiding reminders of serious illness
Evidence-based help
Cognitive behavioral therapy, for health anxiety and related illness anxiety

What the term means

Nosophobia is an established term in the medical literature, also called disease phobia. It refers to a persistent fear of contracting or having a dangerous disease, and the fear is often focused on a specific serious illness. In plain English, it is a persistent fear of developing a specific serious disease.

The term is descriptive. Health anxiety and illness anxiety disorder are related to it and overlap with it, but the name does not settle a diagnosis. A clinician has to assess which diagnosis is appropriate. It cannot be inferred from a label.

Sources: [1] [2]

How a sensation becomes an alarm

Bodily sensations and health information about disease can become cues for catastrophic interpretation. People may misinterpret a sensation as a sign of serious illness and overestimate the threat.

Anxiety itself can cause a racing heartbeat, and that heartbeat may then be misinterpreted as illness. A strong feeling of alarm does not by itself establish that a disease is present.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Checking, relief and persistence

The cognitive behavioral model of health anxiety links a chain of steps: a bodily cue, a catastrophic interpretation about illness, anxiety, and then checking, reassurance-seeking or avoidance. Those bring short-term relief. The fear persists because the feared beliefs remain untested. This is the model for health anxiety, a related problem. It is a model, not every person's pathway.

People may repeatedly check their bodies, search for health information, seek reassurance, or avoid reminders of serious illness and medical settings.

Sources: [2] [3]

Therapy and clinical care

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is evidence-based help for health anxiety and related illness anxiety. It addresses catastrophic beliefs, vigilance toward the body, excessive checking, reassurance seeking and avoidance.

The sources point to seeing a clinician when health worries impair daily life, and they describe assessment and appropriate care as important. Reducing excessive checking belongs inside a care plan. It does not mean abandoning appropriate medical care. Educational material, this infographic included, does not diagnose illness.

Sources: [2] [3]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Somniphobia — Extreme Fear of Sleep

Somniphobia is an extreme fear of sleep. Even the thought of going to sleep may provoke extreme anxiety, and fear of sleep is not identical to insomnia.

At a glance

Meaning
Extreme fear of sleep
Anticipatory anxiety
Thoughts of going to sleep can be enough to provoke fear
Possible symptoms
Palpitations, chest tightness, trembling; responses vary between people
Not identical to
Insomnia
PTSD research
Fear of sleep related to nightmares and hypervigilance in a studied PTSD sample
Help
Talking therapies including CBT can help phobias

Fear of sleep and anticipation

Somniphobia means extreme fear of sleep. Even thinking of going to sleep may provoke extreme anxiety. Anticipatory anxiety means anxiety before the feared situation, and thoughts of going to sleep can be sufficient to provoke fear. Phobia symptoms can include palpitations, chest tightness and trembling. Responses vary between people.

Sources: [1] [2]

What studies of PTSD found

In fear of sleep related to post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anticipated nightmares and the inability to remain vigilant while asleep can contribute. This is not an explanation for every person. Hypervigilance means remaining on guard. In studied adults with PTSD and insomnia, fear of sleep is associated with greater hypervigilance.

Fear of sleep is not identical to insomnia. In the studied PTSD sample, it related to nightmares and hypervigilance, not to classic insomnia symptoms.

Avoiding sleep-related reminders may occur in trauma-related fear. Reliance on avoidance can make trauma symptoms worse and impede recovery.

Sources: [3] [4]

Fear, danger and assessment

Fear can be disproportionate to a threat. The intensity of a fear response is not itself evidence of current danger. Real sleep symptoms warrant individual assessment.

Sources: [2] [3]

Therapy and the limits of one trial

Talking therapies, including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), can help phobias. A health professional is relevant when symptoms affect daily life. In a trial of adults with both PTSD and insomnia, cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) reduced fear of sleep. That finding is specific to the group studied. It is not a universal promise.

Sources: [2] [3]

Thanatophobia — Fear of Death

Thanatophobia is an established term for fear of death. Awareness of mortality is common, and not all worry about death is illness. Distress and disruption of daily life are what warrant assessment.

At a glance

Meaning
Fear of death
Status
An established term; not presented as a separate diagnosis
Possible reminders
Death-related conversations and news; thoughts of one's own death
Possible symptoms
Palpitations, dizziness, trembling; symptoms differ between people
Approach that can help
CBT, addressing unhelpful beliefs and avoidance

A common awareness, an established term

Thanatophobia is an established term for fear of death. Death anxiety is studied across multiple mental health conditions, and the term is not presented here as a separate diagnosis.

Awareness of mortality is common. Distress and disruption of daily life warrant assessment. It is not assumed that all death-related worry is illness.

Sources: [1] [2] [3] [4]

Reminders and the body's alarm

Death-related conversations and news can act as reminders that provoke death anxiety, and thoughts of one's own death can be feared. Phobic anxiety may include palpitations, dizziness and trembling. Symptoms differ between people.

Perceived threat can exceed the current situation. A reminder or a frightening thought is not itself evidence of imminent death.

Sources: [3] [4]

Avoidance and short-term relief

Avoiding death-related reminders can be an unhelpful coping behavior that maintains death anxiety. Short-term relief is not the same thing as lasting recovery.

Sources: [2] [4]

Support planned with a clinician

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can reduce death anxiety by addressing unhelpful beliefs and avoidance. Individualized professional assessment is relevant when fear disrupts life.

The sources say any exposure work should be planned collaboratively with a trained clinician, using safe, gradual steps and not forced confrontation, and that normal medical care should be maintained.

Sources: [2] [3] [4]

This page is general information for learning. It is not a diagnosis or medical advice. Talk to a health professional about your own situation.

Tokophobia — Severe Fear of Childbirth

Tokophobia is an established term for a severe or phobic fear of childbirth, which is different from ordinary uncertainty about birth. The anxiety may occur even when someone wants a child.

At a glance

Meaning
Severe or phobic fear of childbirth
Primary tokophobia
Can occur without prior experience of birth
Secondary tokophobia
Can follow a difficult or traumatic birth
Possible symptoms
Rapid heartbeat, muscle tension, disturbed sleep, panic symptoms
Support can include
Midwife or obstetrician, perinatal mental-health referral, therapy such as CBT, collaborative birth plan

More than ordinary uncertainty

Tokophobia is an established term for severe or phobic fear of childbirth. It is not ordinary uncertainty about birth. Anxiety may occur even when someone wants a child, and symptoms and experiences vary.

Primary tokophobia can occur without prior experience of birth. Secondary tokophobia can follow a difficult or traumatic birth.

Sources: [1] [2]

What the fear can involve

Anticipatory anxiety can increase during pregnancy. Thoughts about birth, negative accounts of birth and memories of a traumatic previous birth may be associated with fear. Fears may focus on harm to the parent or baby. Anxiety symptoms can include a rapid heartbeat, muscle tension, disturbed sleep and panic symptoms.

Avoidance can involve not talking or thinking about birth and avoiding antenatal education. Isolation and feeling unsupported can also occur.

Sources: [1]

Maternity and mental-health support

Guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence is that people with tokophobia should be offered a discussion with a professional experienced in supporting this fear. Support can include speaking with a midwife or obstetrician, a perinatal mental-health referral, psychological therapy such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), and a collaborative birth plan that includes pain-relief and birth options.

Maternity teams discuss birth options and develop plans that account for both physical and mental health. Fear alone does not measure an individual's obstetric risk. Treatment is individualized to the symptoms and the anxiety condition, and education is not an individual diagnosis.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]
